title: What plants need underground: air, minerals and helpers in the soil

summary.text: A brinjal plant in a big pot starts to droop and turn yellow. The family waters the plant more and adds fertiliser, and the plant gets worse. What is wrong? Your child pours water onto dry soil and sees bubbles of air rush out, and finds that between a third and a half of soil is gaps. Roots need that air as much as they need water. Then comes the rest of what happens underground: about a dozen minerals that a plant needs in tiny amounts, the rule that the mineral in shortest supply limits how well the plant grows, bacteria that make fertiliser inside bean roots, and fungi that trade with trees. Some of it is well known, and some of it scientists still argue about.
summary.art: A brinjal plant with yellow leaves in a pot standing in a saucer of water, and a cutaway of the pot showing pale roots drowning in soaked soil.

intro.hook: You water a drooping plant, and they droop more. You water again, and they get worse. How can more water make a thirsty-looking plant sicker?
intro.text: A plant that droops looks as if they are dry, so most of us reach for the watering can. But the drooping can also come from too much water. Roots are alive. They need food, water, and air to breathe, just as you do. In this unit you pour water onto dry soil and find out how much air hides between the grains. Then you look at the other things a plant needs from the soil. The plant needs only small amounts of them, but cannot do without them. Last, you look at the bacteria and fungi that help the plant get them.
intro.art: A hand pouring water from a jug onto dry soil in a clear glass, with silver bubbles of air rising from the soil.

outcomes: I can explain that roots need air as well as water, and why a pot with standing water can kill a plant.
I can measure how much air is in a soil, and compare two kinds of soil, and packed soil with loose soil.
I can name the three main minerals plants take from soil, nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, and say what each is used for.
I can run a fair test with seedlings in plain water and in water with minerals, and explain what I see.
I can explain the idea of the shortest plank: the mineral in shortest supply sets how well a plant grows.
I can explain how bean-family plants and bacteria trade sugar for nitrogen, and why farmers grow dal after rice.
I can say what scientists know about the fungi on roots, and what they still argue about.
I can say what scientists agree about, who found out each part, and what is still unknown.

terms.meaning: A simple substance from the soil, such as nitrate or potassium, that a plant takes in through the roots, dissolved in water. A plant needs only small amounts, but cannot grow without them.
terms.example: Nitrate is a mineral nutrient that a plant uses to make chlorophyll and proteins.
terms.art: A root hair taking in water with tiny coloured specks dissolved in it.

terms.meaning: An element that plants need to make chlorophyll and proteins. About 78 parts in every 100 of the air is nitrogen gas, but a plant cannot use the gas. They take it in as nitrate or ammonium from the soil.
terms.example: A plant short of nitrogen turns pale yellow-green, starting with the oldest leaves.
terms.art: A bottle of air with 78 dots of nitrogen out of 100, and a plant with yellow lower leaves beside it.

terms.meaning: A mineral that holds nitrogen in a form that dissolves in water. Roots take it in easily. Bacteria in the soil make nitrate from dead plants and animals.
terms.example: Compost slowly releases nitrate that a vegetable plant can use.
terms.art: A single nitrate molecule drawn as one blue ball with three red balls, drifting towards a root.

terms.meaning: An element that plants use to build their energy carriers, their DNA and their roots and flowers. They take it in from the soil as phosphate.
terms.example: A plant short of phosphorus grows slowly and some leaves turn dark green or purple.
terms.art: A young plant with small roots and purple-tinted leaves next to a healthy plant with a big root system.

terms.meaning: An element that helps the stomata open and close, and helps the plant manage water. It also helps move sugar around.
terms.example: A plant short of potassium often has yellow or brown edges on the older leaves.
terms.art: A leaf with brown scorched edges and a healthy green leaf beside it.

terms.meaning: A substance added to soil to give plants minerals. It can be made from natural things, such as cow dung, or made in a factory. A plant takes up the same simple minerals from either.
terms.example: A farmer spreads urea on a paddy field to give nitrogen.
terms.art: A farmer scattering fertiliser over a green paddy field from a basket.

terms.meaning: Plant waste, such as vegetable peels and dry leaves, that has been rotted by bacteria, fungi and worms into a dark, crumbly material that feeds plants.
terms.example: A heap of kitchen peels and dry leaves turns into compost in a few weeks to months.
terms.art: A compost bin with kitchen peels at the top and dark crumbly compost at the bottom.

terms.meaning: The dark, spongy part of soil made from well-rotted plants and animals. It holds water and minerals like a sponge.
terms.example: The dark top layer of a forest floor is rich in humus.
terms.art: A cutaway of forest soil with a dark top layer of humus and a pale layer of sand and clay below.

terms.meaning: The air that fills the gaps between the grains of soil. Roots and soil living things use the oxygen in it to respire.
terms.example: When water is poured onto dry soil, soil air escapes as bubbles.
terms.art: A magnified drawing of soil grains with white gaps between them, labelled air, and a root hair among them.

terms.meaning: Soaked so full of water that the gaps in the soil have no air left. A waterlogged soil is a danger for the roots of most plants.
terms.example: A pot with a blocked hole becomes waterlogged after heavy rain.
terms.art: A pot with water standing in a full saucer, and brown mushy roots seen through the glass.

terms.meaning: A tiny hair on a young root, thinner than a thread. Root hairs take in water and minerals, and spread the root out between the grains of soil.
terms.example: A moong sprout has a fuzz of white root hairs, which you can see with a magnifying glass.
terms.art: A moong sprout root with a fuzz of white root hairs, enlarged in a circle.

terms.meaning: Growing plants with their roots in water that holds dissolved minerals, and no soil. It is also called hydroponics.
terms.example: Lettuce can be grown in trays of mineral water on a rooftop farm, with no soil at all.
terms.art: Rows of lettuce plants with their roots hanging in a shallow tray of water.

terms.meaning: Water with minerals dissolved in it in the right amounts for a plant to take in.
terms.example: A few drops of liquid plant fertiliser in a litre of water make a nutrient solution.
terms.art: A bottle of liquid fertiliser dripping one drop into a jar of water.

terms.meaning: A plant of the bean family, which grows seeds in pods. Dals, groundnuts, peas, beans and tamarind are legumes. They can get nitrogen with the help of bacteria in their roots.
terms.example: Moong, chana, tur and groundnut are all legumes.
terms.art: A row of pods: moong, groundnut, pea, tamarind and tur, each cut open to show seeds.

terms.meaning: A small lump on the root of a legume, where helpful bacteria live. Inside, the bacteria turn nitrogen gas from the air into a form the plant can use.
terms.example: A groundnut plant pulled from the field has dozens of pale lumps on the roots. When you cut one, it is pink inside.
terms.art: A groundnut root with small round nodules, and one nodule cut open to show a pink inside.

terms.meaning: Turning nitrogen gas from the air into a form that plants can use. Some bacteria do it. Lightning does a little. Factories do it too, to make fertiliser.
terms.example: A bean plant's root bacteria fix nitrogen. A fertiliser factory also fixes nitrogen, using high heat and pressure.
terms.art: Three pictures of nitrogen fixing: a lightning flash, a root nodule with bacteria, and a fertiliser factory.

terms.meaning: A partnership between a fungus and a plant root. The fungus spreads thin threads through the soil and brings minerals and water to the plant. The plant gives the fungus sugar. The word means 'fungus root'.
terms.example: Most trees in a forest have fungi living on and inside their roots.
terms.art: A tree root wrapped in white fungal threads that spread out through the soil, with arrows of sugar going in and minerals coming out.

terms.meaning: The mineral that is in shortest supply for a plant, which sets how well the plant can grow. Adding more of another mineral does not help until this one is supplied.
terms.example: If a soil has plenty of potassium but very little nitrogen, adding potassium will not help the crop. Nitrogen is the limiting nutrient.
terms.art: A barrel with planks of different heights labelled nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, and water spilling over the shortest.

terms.meaning: Not having enough of something. A plant with a mineral deficiency shows signs, such as yellow or purple leaves, that point to what is missing.
terms.example: Pale yellow older leaves are often a sign of a nitrogen deficiency.
terms.art: Four leaves in a row: pale yellow, purple, brown-edged and yellow with green veins.

terms.meaning: Growing different crops in the same field in turns, season after season. Growing a legume in between helps put nitrogen back into the soil.
terms.example: A farmer grows rice in the wet season and a dal such as black gram in the dry season on the same field.
terms.art: A field divided into four plots with rice, black gram, groundnut and wheat, and arrows rotating between them.

terms.meaning: A tiny floating water fern, with bacteria living in the leaves that fix nitrogen. Farmers in Asia have grown it in paddy fields to feed the rice.
terms.example: A green mat of azolla can cover a paddy field in a few weeks.
terms.art: A paddy field with a thick green mat of tiny azolla ferns floating between the rice plants.

terms.meaning: Long air channels inside the stems and roots of plants that grow in mud and water. They carry air down from the leaves to the roots. The word is said 'air-EN-kim-ah'.
terms.example: A slice of lotus stem has big round holes in it. They are air channels.
terms.art: A slice of lotus stem showing a ring of holes, with arrows of air moving down the stem into mud.

explanations.concept: Roots need air: the gaps in soil
explanations.definition: Soil is not solid. It is made of grains with gaps between them. A good soil has between a third and a half of its volume as gaps. The gaps hold air and water, and roots breathe the air.
explanations.description: Pick up a handful of soil, and it seems like one solid thing. Pour water onto it and bubbles of air rush out. That air was in the gaps between the grains. In a loose garden soil, the gaps can be nearly half of the volume. Roots grow into these gaps. A root is made of living cells, and every living cell respires. The root cells use oxygen to break down sugar that the leaves sent down, and they give out carbon dioxide. The oxygen comes from the air in the gaps. When the gaps are full of water, or squashed shut by trampling, the oxygen runs out. The root cells cannot get energy, and they begin to die. A plant can then droop and turn yellow even though there is plenty of water. The grains hold the plant up, but the gaps are where the roots live and breathe.
examples: A garden path that people walk on every day has packed, hard soil with few gaps, so few plants grow there.
A loose soil with lots of dry leaves in it has many gaps, and earthworms keep making more.
Gently digging the soil in a pot opens up gaps, so the roots can breathe.
explanations.art: A magnified cutaway of soil showing round grains in brown, white gaps between them, and a root hair with a tiny oxygen arrow going in.
explanations.context: Roots are alive and need to breathe. This card shows where the roots find air in the soil.

explanations.concept: Drowning roots: why too much water kills
explanations.definition: In a waterlogged soil, water fills the gaps and pushes out the air. Oxygen moves through water thousands of times more slowly than through air, so the roots run out of oxygen and die.
explanations.description: When you water a plant, water fills the gaps, and the extra drains out through the bottom. If the pot has no hole, or the hole is blocked, or the saucer stays full, the water stays. Oxygen can still dissolve into the water, but it spreads through water thousands of times more slowly than through air. The roots and the soil bacteria use up the little oxygen there is. Soon the roots have none. Roots without oxygen cannot take in water or minerals, so the leaves droop, as if the plant were thirsty. Bacteria that do not need oxygen start to grow and make sour, rotten-egg smells, and the roots turn brown and soft. This is called root rot. Some plants have found ways around it. Rice, lotus and mangroves have long air channels in their stems and roots. They carry air down from the leaves to the roots in the mud. Mangroves in the Sundarbans also push up pencil-like roots above the mud that act like snorkels.
examples: A potted plant left in a saucer of water during the northeast monsoon often turns yellow and droops.
A paddy plant grows well in a flooded field because air flows down inside the stem to the roots.
A brinjal or chilli plant dies in a flooded field in a few days, since they have no air channels.
explanations.art: Two pots side by side. One pot drains freely and has white healthy roots. The other stands in a saucer of water and has brown roots and a drooping plant.
explanations.context: A drooping plant is often thought to be thirsty. This card shows how too much water can kill a plant from below.

explanations.concept: More than water and light: the mineral nutrients
explanations.definition: Besides water, air and light, a plant needs about a dozen or more minerals from the soil. Three are needed in the biggest amounts: nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. Others, such as iron, are needed in tiny amounts.
explanations.description: A plant builds their body from carbon dioxide and water, but that is not enough. Chlorophyll needs nitrogen to be made, and a magnesium atom sits at the middle of every chlorophyll molecule. The plant also needs iron to make chlorophyll. Proteins need nitrogen and sulphur. The energy carriers in a cell, and the DNA, need phosphorus. Potassium helps the guard cells open and close the stomata. Calcium helps hold the cell walls together. Plants take these minerals from the soil water through their roots, as tiny dissolved bits called ions. The three biggest needs, nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, are often called N, P and K. They are the three numbers on a bag of fertiliser. A plant needs very small amounts of others, such as zinc, copper, boron and manganese. But a tiny amount is still a necessary amount. Without any one of them, the plant cannot complete their life.
examples: The three numbers on a bag of fertiliser, such as 20-10-10, tell how much nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium it holds.
A mineral needed in tiny amounts, like iron, is still essential. Without it, new leaves come out yellow.
Spinach is rich in iron, which the plant took from the soil.
explanations.art: A plant with arrows from the roots to the leaves labelled with N, P, K, Mg and Fe, and a small picture of what each one is used for.
explanations.context: Plants need light, water and warmth. This card adds the things the roots take from the soil.

explanations.concept: Reading the leaves: clues to what is missing
explanations.definition: A plant short of a mineral shows it in their leaves. Where the sign appears, and what it looks like, are clues to what the plant is missing.
explanations.description: Some minerals can be moved around inside a plant, and some cannot. Nitrogen can move. When there is too little, the plant pulls nitrogen out of the oldest leaves to feed the new growth, so the old leaves turn pale yellow first. Potassium also moves, so a shortage often shows as yellow or brown edges on the older leaves. Phosphorus shortage can make older leaves dark green or purple. Iron cannot move around once it has been put in a leaf. So with too little iron, the newest leaves turn yellow while the veins stay green. These patterns are only clues, not proof. Several different problems can make a leaf yellow, including too much water, too little light and root rot. A good plant doctor looks at which leaves are affected, then checks the roots and the soil before deciding.
examples: Old, lower leaves of a tomato plant turn pale yellow first. This is a clue for nitrogen.
New leaves on a lemon plant turn yellow with green veins. This is a clue for iron.
Yellow leaves from the bottom of a potted plant in a full saucer may be root rot instead.
explanations.art: A tomato plant with pale yellow lower leaves and green top leaves, and a lemon plant with its top leaves yellow and the veins green.
explanations.context: A plant cannot tell you what is wrong, but their leaves can. This card shows how to read the clues.

explanations.concept: The shortest plank: the limiting nutrient
explanations.definition: A plant's growth is limited by the mineral that is in the shortest supply. Adding more of the other minerals does not help until the shortest one is supplied.
explanations.description: Think of a wooden barrel made of planks of different heights. You can only fill the barrel as high as the shortest plank, because water spills over it. A plant is like that. Suppose the soil has lots of phosphorus and potassium but very little nitrogen. The plant grows only as well as the nitrogen allows. Pouring on more phosphorus does nothing. This idea is called the law of the minimum. A German agricultural scientist named Carl Sprengel worked it out in 1828, and the chemist Justus von Liebig made it famous in the 1840s. Today it is often called Liebig's law, though Sprengel was first. Farmers use it. They test the soil, find the mineral in shortest supply and add only that. This saves money, and it saves the soil and rivers from extra minerals that the crop cannot use.
examples: A farmer's soil test shows plenty of potassium and phosphorus but low nitrogen. She adds a nitrogen fertiliser, and the crop improves.
A house plant with pale leaves does not need more water. They may need a few drops of fertiliser with nitrogen.
explanations.art: A barrel with five planks of different heights labelled N, P, K, Ca and Fe, with water filling to the shortest plank, N.
explanations.context: Some minerals can be plentiful while one is short. This card shows why the shortest one decides how well a plant grows.

explanations.concept: Growing without soil: the water culture test
explanations.definition: A plant can grow with no soil at all, if their roots are in water that holds the right minerals and enough air. This shows that the plant's food is made in the leaves, and from the soil they need only minerals and support.
explanations.description: Around 1860, the German plant scientists Julius Sachs and Wilhelm Knop grew plants in glass jars, with their roots in water. They put into the water only a few simple minerals: salts of nitrogen, potassium, calcium, magnesium, phosphorus, sulphur and iron. There was no soil and no rotting humus. The plants grew well and made seeds. This showed that plants do not need humus as food, as many farmers then believed. It also showed that soil provides only water, minerals and support. Today, this idea is used in water culture farming, also called hydroponics. Lettuce, tomatoes and herbs are grown on trays and pipes with their roots in a flowing mineral solution. A water culture grower must pump air into the water, or leave an air gap, because roots in water still need to breathe.
examples: A tray of lettuce on a rooftop, with roots hanging in flowing mineral water.
A money plant that lives in a glass of water for a year, taking the tiny amounts of minerals they need from the water.
explanations.art: A glass jar with a plant held over water by a collar, white roots hanging in the water, with a small bubble stone adding air.
explanations.context: If the soil only gives minerals and support, a plant should grow without soil. This card shows that it can.

explanations.concept: Nitrogen: plenty in the air, but hard to use
explanations.definition: Air is about 78 parts in 100 nitrogen gas, but plants cannot use the gas. Nitrogen must be 'fixed', that is, joined to other atoms, before roots can take it in. Bacteria, lightning and factories fix nitrogen.
explanations.description: Nitrogen gas is made of two nitrogen atoms joined by a very strong bond. Plants and animals cannot break it. So a plant can be surrounded by nitrogen and still starve for it. Nitrogen has to be fixed first, into forms such as nitrate and ammonium. There are three ways it happens. Lightning does a little, because its heat joins nitrogen and oxygen, and rain carries the result to the soil. Bacteria do much more. Some live free in the soil, some live in lumps on the roots of legumes, and some live inside the tiny water fern azolla. And since the early 1900s, factories do it too. Two German chemists, Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch, worked out how to make ammonia from nitrogen gas and hydrogen at high heat and pressure. Fertiliser made this way is estimated to feed roughly half of all people alive today. The same chemistry was also used to make explosives, and Haber's later wartime work with poison gas was a terrible use of science.
examples: Urea in a bag of fertiliser is made from factory nitrogen.
Rain after a thunderstorm carries a little fixed nitrogen to the soil.
Dead leaves and dung rot into nitrate that roots can take in.
explanations.art: A bottle of air full of nitrogen dots, with three arrows pointing to a lightning bolt, a bean root with nodules and a fertiliser factory.
explanations.context: The air is mostly nitrogen, yet plants run short of it. This card explains why, and how nitrogen gets to roots.

explanations.concept: Beans and their bacteria: root nodules
explanations.definition: Plants of the bean family, called legumes, grow lumps on their roots called nodules. Helpful bacteria called rhizobia live in the nodules. The bacteria fix nitrogen for the plant, and the plant gives them sugar.
explanations.description: Dig up a groundnut or a pea plant with their roots, and you will see small round lumps on the roots. These are nodules. Inside each nodule live millions of bacteria, called rhizobia. The plant gives them sugar made by photosynthesis. In return, the bacteria turn nitrogen gas from the air into ammonia that the plant can use. A healthy nodule is pink inside, because it holds a red substance that carries oxygen, a bit like the red in blood. This is a trade, and both sides gain. It was worked out in the 1880s by two German scientists, Hermann Hellriegel and Hermann Wilfarth, and the bacteria were first grown in a dish by a Dutch scientist named Martinus Beijerinck. Rice and wheat use up nitrogen. Farmers in India have long grown dals such as tur, moong, urad and chana in turns with them. The legume leaves some nitrogen behind in the soil for the next crop.
examples: A groundnut plant pulled from a field has dozens of nodules. When you cut one open, it is pink.
A farmer grows black gram after rice, so the next rice crop needs less fertiliser.
A green manure plant such as dhaincha is ploughed into the soil to put nitrogen back.
explanations.art: A groundnut plant pulled from the soil with round nodules on the roots, and one nodule cut in half to show a pink inside and tiny bacteria.
explanations.context: Some plants make their own nitrogen fertiliser with help. This card shows the trade inside a bean's roots.

explanations.definition: Most land plants have fungi living on or inside their roots. The fungus spreads thin threads through the soil and brings the plant water and minerals, especially phosphorus. The plant gives the fungus sugar. This partnership is called mycorrhiza.
explanations.description: A root is thick compared with a fungus thread, which is much finer than a root hair. A fungus can reach into tiny gaps between grains that a root cannot, and can spread far beyond the root. Phosphorus does not move easily through soil, and a root soon uses up all the phosphorus close to it. The fungus brings more from farther away. In exchange, the plant sends the fungus a share of the sugar from their leaves. Scientists estimate that most land plants, perhaps eight or nine in every ten kinds, have fungus partners like this. The partnership was named mycorrhiza in 1885 by a German scientist named Albert Bernhard Frank. Some early land plants that lived hundreds of millions of years ago already had fungus partners, which suggests that plants may have needed fungi to move onto land at all. Mushrooms you see on the ground are only the fruit of fungi whose threads spread far underground.
examples: Mushrooms appearing under a tree after rain are the fruits of fungi linked to the tree's roots.
Plants grown in sterilised soil, with no fungi, often grow smaller and take up less phosphorus.
explanations.art: A tree root wrapped in a white web of fungus threads that spread far out between soil grains, with sugar arrows going down and mineral arrows coming up.
explanations.context: Roots do not work alone. This card shows the fungus partners that help most plants to feed.

explanations.concept: Compost and humus: dead things feed the living
explanations.definition: Compost is plant and animal waste rotted by bacteria, fungi and worms. It turns into humus and minerals that plants can take up, and it opens up the soil so that it holds air and water.
explanations.description: Nothing in nature is waste. A fallen leaf, a vegetable peel or cow dung is food for decomposers: bacteria, fungi, worms, beetles and tiny soil creatures. They break the dead material down. They use some of it for their own bodies and energy, and leave the rest as simple minerals that roots can take in, such as nitrate and phosphate. What remains is a dark, spongy material called humus. Humus does three jobs. It holds minerals so that rain does not wash them away. It holds water like a sponge. And it makes the soil crumbly, with lots of gaps for air. This is why gardeners add compost, and why farmers in India have used cow dung manure and vermicompost for centuries. A heap of compost can get warm, because the decomposers are respiring fast and giving off heat. Rotting is not the end of a leaf. It is the leaf's next job.
examples: Kitchen peels and dry leaves turn into dark, earthy-smelling compost in a few weeks to months.
Vermicompost is made by earthworms eating waste and leaving rich castings behind.
A forest has no farmer and no fertiliser bag, and trees still grow, because the leaf litter is recycled.
explanations.art: A heap of dry leaves and peels on the left, earthworms and fungus threads in the middle, and dark crumbly compost in a plant pot on the right.
explanations.context: Where do the minerals in soil come from? This card shows how dead leaves and dung return to plants.

explanations.concept: Too much of a good thing: when fertiliser harms
explanations.definition: A plant needs minerals, but too much fertiliser can harm them. Strong fertiliser salts can pull water out of the roots and scorch the leaves, and extra minerals that the crop cannot use wash into rivers and lakes.
explanations.description: Fertiliser is made of salts. When there is a lot of salt in the soil water, the roots find it hard to take in water, and may even lose water. The leaf edges turn brown and crispy. Farmers call this fertiliser burn. It is common in pots, where a strong dose has nowhere to go. A small dose, often, works better than a big one at once. Another problem happens downstream. Rain can wash extra nitrate and phosphate off fields and into ponds and rivers. There they can feed a huge growth of algae, called a bloom, which later rots and uses up the oxygen so that fish die. Careful farmers use only what the crop needs, and place it where the roots are. Compost and manure release minerals slowly. The Class 4 unit on photosynthesis tells how an algae bloom can use up the oxygen in a pond.
examples: A potted plant gets brown leaf edges after a double dose of liquid fertiliser.
Green, smelly water at the mouth of a river after heavy rain can come from fertiliser washed off the fields.
explanations.art: A pot plant with brown crispy leaf edges beside a bottle of fertiliser with a large dose spilling, and a green pond downstream.
explanations.context: If a little fertiliser helps, more may seem better. This card shows why it is not.

explanations.concept: A handful of soil is alive
explanations.definition: Healthy soil is full of living things: bacteria, fungi, worms, mites and tiny animals. They recycle dead material, make minerals available to roots, and keep the soil loose with gaps.
explanations.description: A teaspoon of healthy soil can hold hundreds of millions of bacteria and long threads of fungi. Larger animals live there too: earthworms, ants, beetles, termites and tiny mites. They are the soil's workforce. Earthworms eat soil and dead leaves, and their burrows let air and water down to the roots. Charles Darwin spent about forty years watching earthworms, and in 1881 he published a book about them. He worked out that worms bring many tonnes of soil to the surface of a field each year, and that they slowly bury old stones and even ruined walls. Many people laughed at the idea of a book about worms, but it sold very well. Bacteria and fungi do the rest. They turn dead matter into minerals and humus. When the soil is poisoned with too much chemical, or packed hard by machines, this life dies, and the soil becomes tired. So a farmer's soil is more than a heap of grains. It is also full of living things that need looking after.
examples: Little heaps of soil on the ground after rain are worm casts, soil that earthworms have passed through their bodies.
A rotting log on a forest floor is crawling with beetles, fungi and bacteria.
explanations.art: A cutaway of soil showing an earthworm, fungus threads, beetles, ants, mites and a root, each labelled.
explanations.context: Soil is more than grains. This card shows the living things that make it work.

explanations.concept: Do roots decide where to grow?
explanations.description: Roots do not grow at random. They grow towards water. They grow thicker where there are minerals. They bend away from salt and from poisons, and they steer round rocks. A root tip senses gravity, moisture, touch, chemicals and even the roots of other plants, and then decides which way to grow. In 1880, Charles Darwin and his son Francis wrote that the tip of a root seems to act like the brain of a simple animal, directing the root's movements. Today, scientists agree that roots sense and respond. They argue about what to call it.
examples: A root grows more branches into a patch of soil rich in minerals than into a poor patch.
A root that meets a stone turns and grows around it.

perspectives.who: Plant scientists such as Stefano Mancuso, Frantisek Baluska and others
perspectives.explanation: Roots gather information, compare it, remember it and choose. This is a kind of thinking. Roots and shoots are intelligent, in their own way, and have no need of a brain.

perspectives.who: Other plant scientists, such as Lincoln Taiz and colleagues
perspectives.explanation: Roots do respond in clever ways, but these are chemical responses to signals, like an automatic system. There is no reason to call it thinking or choosing, and no evidence for awareness.

explanations.art: A root tip approaching a rock and a patch of rich soil, bending away from the rock and branching into the rich patch.
explanations.context: A root has no eyes and no brain, yet finds their way. This card shows how scientists describe what a root does, and where they disagree.

explanations.concept: Do trees share food through fungus networks?
explanations.description: Because many trees in a forest share the same fungus, some scientists have asked if the fungus threads form a network between trees. Could the network pass sugar, water or warning signals from one tree to another? In 1997, a team led by the Canadian forest scientist Suzanne Simard reported that carbon moved between young trees of two different kinds in a forest, and that fungi might be the link. The idea was called the wood wide web, and it became famous in books and films. The picture of old 'mother trees' feeding their children through the network moved many people. Other scientists now say that some of these claims have gone further than the evidence.
examples: In experiments, carbon marked with a tracer was found to move between nearby trees in a forest.
Seedlings that share a fungus with an old tree sometimes grow better than seedlings that do not.

perspectives.who: Suzanne Simard and scientists who agree with her
perspectives.explanation: Fungus networks link trees and move carbon, water and signals between them. Older trees can help seedlings. A forest is more like a community than a crowd of single competing trees.

perspectives.who: Justine Karst, Melanie Jones, Jason Hoeksema and other scientists, in 2023
perspectives.explanation: Fungus threads do link roots, and some carbon does move. But there is not enough evidence that the movement is big enough to help seedlings survive, or that trees do this on purpose to help their kin. Some popular claims have run ahead of the evidence.

explanations.art: A forest with trees whose roots are joined by white thread-like fungi, with glowing dots moving along the threads, and a question mark above.
explanations.context: A forest is often described as a connected community. This card shows what has been found and what is still argued.

explanations.concept: The Green Revolution: more food, and new costs
explanations.description: In the 1960s, India had a food shortage and relied on grain from other countries. Scientists, including Norman Borlaug in Mexico and M. S. Swaminathan in India, helped bring in new short-stalked varieties of wheat and rice. These plants put more of their energy into grain, and did not fall over when given a lot of fertiliser. With fertiliser, irrigation and new seed, harvests rose steeply, and India became much less dependent on imported grain. This was called the Green Revolution. It also brought costs. Farmers bought seed, fertiliser and pumps, and many took on debts. In some regions, the water in the ground fell, and soils became tired. Extra fertiliser flowed into rivers. Scientists and farmers still disagree about the balance.
examples: In Punjab and Haryana, wheat and rice harvests rose steeply, and the water table in many places has fallen.
Newer ideas, such as growing dal in turns with cereals and adding compost, aim to keep the high yields while caring for the soil.

perspectives.explanation: It saved many people from hunger. Without new varieties and fertiliser, there could not have been enough food for India's growing population.
It made farmers depend on costly seed and fertiliser, drained the groundwater, tired the soil and pushed aside older crops such as millets. The benefits were not shared equally.

explanations.art: Two fields side by side: a tall thin traditional wheat plant bending over, and a short strong modern wheat plant carrying heavy grain, with a fertiliser bag and a water pump in the corner.
explanations.context: Fertiliser changed how India feeds itself. This card shows what it gave, what it cost and why people still argue about it.

agreed.text: Roots need oxygen to respire. Waterlogged soil, in which the gaps are full of water, kills the roots of most plants.
agreed.evidence: Roots in water without oxygen stop growing and die within days. Plants with air channels, such as rice and lotus, survive floods because the channels carry air down to the roots.

agreed.text: Plants need at least a dozen minerals from the soil, in small amounts. Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are needed in the largest amounts.
agreed.evidence: Plants grown in water culture grow well with the right minerals and fail when any one is left out. Plant ash contains the same minerals.

agreed.text: Plants do not need humus or soil as food. They need minerals, water, air and light, and make their own food by photosynthesis.
agreed.evidence: Since about 1860, plants have been grown in water with only mineral salts, and have made leaves, flowers and seeds.

agreed.text: A plant's growth is held back by the mineral that is in shortest supply.
agreed.evidence: In farmers' trials, one mineral at a time is added to a soil. The crop grows better only when the mineral in shortest supply is added.

agreed.text: Bacteria in the root nodules of legumes fix nitrogen for the plant, and the plant gives them sugar.
agreed.evidence: Legumes grown in sterile soil make no nodules and grow poorly without nitrogen. When the right bacteria are added, nodules form and the plants thrive. Radioactive and heavy kinds of nitrogen can be followed from the air into the plant.

agreed.text: Most land plants have fungi on or in their roots that bring them minerals, especially phosphorus, in exchange for sugar.
agreed.evidence: Under a microscope, fungus threads can be seen entering root cells. Tracers show phosphorus moving from fungus to plant and carbon moving from plant to fungus.

agreed.text: Too much fertiliser can burn plants and cause algae blooms and fish deaths in water downstream.
agreed.evidence: Scorched leaves are seen on plants given strong doses. Dead zones in lakes and at river mouths have been traced to fertiliser and sewage flowing in.

agreed.text: Soil is full of living things, whose work keeps it loose, rich and full of air.
agreed.evidence: Sterilised soil grows plants poorly. Counts of soil life show hundreds of millions of bacteria in a teaspoon of healthy soil.

challenging.claim: Plants eat soil, or eat the rotting humus in it.
challenging.who: A belief held for centuries, and taught by respected farm scientists in the early 1800s as the humus theory
challenging.for: Plants grow better in dark, rich soil. Farmers who add manure get better crops. It seems natural that the plant eats what is dark and rich.
challenging.against: Plants grown in water with only mineral salts do well. The food of a plant is sugar, made in the leaves. The soil gives water, minerals and support, and manure helps by releasing minerals and by opening the soil.
challenging.context: This card is about an old and common mistake: that a plant's food is the soil.

challenging.claim: A drooping plant is thirsty, so more water always helps.
challenging.who: A habit among many gardeners and families
challenging.for: A dry plant really does droop, and a good watering brings them back.
challenging.against: A plant in soaked soil droops too, because the roots have no air. Giving more water makes it worse. Feel the soil before you water.
challenging.context: This card is about a drooping plant and the urge to water them.

challenging.claim: Air is mostly nitrogen, so plants get all the nitrogen they need from the air.
challenging.who: A reasonable guess that many people make
challenging.for: Nitrogen is by far the largest part of the air, and plants are surrounded by it.
challenging.against: The nitrogen in air is nitrogen gas, whose atoms are locked together very tightly. A plant cannot use it directly. Only fixed forms in the soil, such as nitrate, can be taken in by roots.
challenging.context: This card is about the biggest ingredient of air, and why plants cannot use it.

challenging.claim: One kind of fertiliser, organic or factory-made, is always better than the other.
challenging.who: Different groups of farmers and consumers
challenging.for: Organic manure and compost improve the soil's structure, hold water and feed soil life as well as the plant. Factory fertiliser is cheap, exact and quick, and feeds many people.
challenging.against: A plant takes in the same simple minerals from either kind. Both can be misused. Too much of either can wash into rivers. Manure is slow and may not supply enough nitrogen for very high yields. Factory fertiliser alone, over many years, can leave the soil tired.
challenging.context: This card is about a big argument among farmers: natural versus factory fertiliser.

challenging.claim: Trees in a forest use fungus networks to look after their own young.
challenging.who: A popular idea from books and films, based partly on scientific work
challenging.for: Carbon has been shown to move between trees linked by fungi, and some seedlings near old trees grow better.
challenging.against: Researchers who reviewed the studies in 2023 found that the evidence for many of these claims is weak. Moving a tiny amount of carbon does not show that trees help each other on purpose.
challenging.context: This card asks whether trees really care for their children through the wood wide web.

challenging.claim: The idea of the shortest plank was Justus von Liebig's, so it is right to call it Liebig's law.
challenging.who: Most textbooks, which call it Liebig's law of the minimum
challenging.for: Justus von Liebig was famous, and he put the idea into his best-selling book of 1840.
challenging.against: Carl Sprengel, a less famous German scientist, had written about the idea in 1828. Liebig took the idea and made it famous. Some scientists now say it should be called the Sprengel-Liebig law.
challenging.context: This card asks who deserves the credit for the idea of the shortest plank.

big_questions.q: A drooping plant looks thirsty, yet sometimes the cure is less water. What else in life looks like one problem but is really another?
big_questions.hint: Think about the first thing you reach for when something is wrong. How can you check before you act?

big_questions.q: Soil is half grains and half gaps, and the gaps are where roots live. What does that say about the idea that empty space is nothing?
big_questions.hint: Think of a room, a pot, or a bell. Which part of each is useful?

big_questions.q: A plant needs a tiny bit of iron, but without that tiny bit they cannot make green leaves. Is something small the same as unimportant?
big_questions.hint: Think about the shortest plank in the barrel.

big_questions.q: Beans and bacteria trade sugar for nitrogen, and both do better. Is nature mostly competition, or is it mostly trade?
big_questions.hint: Look for both in a forest. Where do you see each kind? Is one more common?

big_questions.q: Nitrogen is all around us, but plants starve for it. What does that tell us about the difference between having something and being able to use it?
big_questions.hint: Think of money you cannot spend, or a library in a language you cannot read.

big_questions.q: Haber and Bosch's chemistry helped to feed billions of people, and was also used in explosives and war. Can one piece of knowledge be both good and bad?
big_questions.hint: Think about who decides how knowledge is used.

big_questions.q: If trees do share food through fungi, is a forest one living thing or many? And what if they do not?
big_questions.hint: What would you need to see to say that many trees are really one living thing?

big_questions.q: A root decides where to grow without a brain. Where do we draw the line between a living thing that decides and a living thing that is just responding?
big_questions.hint: Think of what you do when you pull your hand away from a hot pan, and what you do when you pick a snack.

big_questions.q: The Green Revolution fed millions and also drained the groundwater. How should we weigh a benefit that comes now against a cost that comes later?
big_questions.hint: Think about who gets the benefit, who pays the cost and when.

big_questions.q: Sprengel found the shortest plank idea first, and Liebig got the name. Who do we forget, and how could we remember them?
big_questions.hint: Think about who writes the books, who sells the most and who speaks the most widely read language.

story.title: Rani on the Balcony
story.note: Revathi, Paati, Appa, Salma Aunty and the plant Rani are made up. The science in the story is real. A plant in soaked soil can droop and yellow, and the roots rot from the bottom. Leaves that have turned yellow do not turn green again. The new leaves are the sign of recovery. A real plant may take longer to recover, or may not recover.
text: Revathi lived with her family in a flat on the third floor in Chennai. The best part of the flat was Paati's balcony. Paati was Revathi's grandmother, and for forty years she had grown things in pots: a tulsi, a curry leaf, a jasmine, and a row of tiny green chillies. But her favourite was a brinjal plant in a big blue pot. She had grown the plant from a seed. She called her Rani, which means queen.
In the summer, Rani had given them eleven purple brinjals, shiny as polished stones. Paati had counted each one. She still talked about the sambar they made from the first one.

Then came October, and the northeast monsoon. The rain came sideways onto the balcony for days. And one morning, Revathi found Rani's leaves turning yellow, from the bottom up. By afternoon they were drooping, as if the plant were tired.
'She is thirsty,' said Paati at once. She filled a steel mug at the tap and gave Rani a good drink. In the evening, she gave her another.

The next day Rani was worse. Appa looked at her over his coffee. 'She is hungry,' he said. He went to the shop at the corner and came back with a packet of plant food. He measured two big spoons of it, double what the packet said, because Rani looked so unwell. 'Strong medicine for a strong queen,' he said.

By the third day, the edges of Rani's leaves had turned brown and crispy. Salma Aunty from the floor below came up to look. 'Too little sun,' she said. 'Move her to the corner.' Paati shook her head. 'She has always been in that spot.'

Revathi did not say anything. She was nine, and her lessons were at home, at the kitchen table. Last week, her mother had given her a clear glass of dry garden soil and a jug of water. 'Pour slowly,' Amma had said. 'Watch.' Revathi had poured, and silver bubbles had streamed out of the soil. 'That is air,' Amma had said. 'Soil is full of gaps, and the gaps are full of air. Roots need to breathe.' They had measured it. Nearly half of the soil had been air.

Now Revathi knelt on the wet balcony tiles and looked at Rani's pot. She pushed a finger into the soil. It was cold, and soaked right down to her knuckle. It had not rained on the pot for hours. Why was it so wet? She sniffed her finger. It smelled sour, like a drain.

She tried to lift the pot. It was heavy, and it sloshed. Under it, the saucer was full of green water, with a tiny mosquito wriggler going up and down. And the hole in the bottom of the pot, which was supposed to let the water out, was plugged tight with a flat piece of broken tile. Appa had put it there, months ago, to stop the soil falling out.
'Paati,' said Revathi. 'Rani is not thirsty.' Paati sighed. 'Kanna, look how she droops. Of course she wants water.'

'When I poured water on the dry soil,' said Revathi, 'bubbles of air came out. The soil has gaps, and the gaps are full of air, and the roots breathe it. Now look. Rani's pot has no gaps with air. They are all full of water. The roots cannot breathe. A plant droops from too little water, and also when the roots are drowning.'
'How do you know?' said Appa. It was a fair question. Revathi thought. 'We can look,' she said. 'If the roots are white and firm, I am wrong. If they are brown and soft, I am right.'

Together, they tipped Rani out onto newspaper. Appa held the pot and Paati held the stem. Revathi took a deep breath. The roots at the top were pale and strong. But the lower part of the root ball was dark brown and slimy, and it smelled terrible.
Nobody spoke for a while. Then Paati said slowly, 'Forty years, I have kept plants. I always thought the roots only drank.'
'They drink and they breathe,' said Revathi. 'Through the same gaps.'

Appa trimmed the brown roots away with kitchen scissors, snip by snip, until only the white ones were left. Revathi mixed new soil in a bucket: garden soil, some sand and a few handfuls of coconut husk, so it would stay loose with plenty of gaps. They put it into a clean pot with three big holes in the bottom, and no tile. Under the pot they put two small bricks, so that the pot would never sit in the water in the saucer. 'And no plant food for two weeks,' said Revathi. 'Drowned roots cannot take it in anyway.'
Then she did something Paati had never done in forty years. She pushed a finger into the soil, two knuckles deep. 'Dry here,' she said. 'Now we can water.' She gave Rani just half a mug.

Ten days later, a small green leaf, the colour of a new parrot, opened at the top of Rani's stem. The old yellow leaves stayed yellow, but Paati did not mind. She snipped them off and put them in the compost.
Salma Aunty came up to see. 'My tulsi is going yellow,' she said. 'Can you look at it, Revathi?'
Paati stood at the balcony with her arms folded. 'Check the finger,' she told her friend, 'not the clock.' She winked at her granddaughter.
story.epiphany: For the parent: roots are alive and breathe. They get oxygen from the air in the gaps between soil grains. When the gaps fill with water, the air is pushed out, and the roots drown. Drooping can mean too much water, and not only too little. In the story, Revathi's clue is the bubbles of air from the soil in a glass, and the proof is the brown, slimy roots. Strong fertiliser on drowned roots makes things worse, because roots with no oxygen cannot take in minerals.
ask: Why can a plant droop from too much water as well as from too little?
How could you tell, without any machine, if a drooping plant is dry or drowning?
Why would giving more fertiliser to a plant with drowned roots not help?
Why does a pot need a hole, and why does a saucer full of water cause trouble?
Soil looks solid. What shows you that it is full of gaps?

A girl kneeling on wet tiles pushing a finger into a soaked pot, with a saucer full of green water and a broken tile plugging the hole.
A girl pouring water from a jug onto dry soil in a clear glass, with silver bubbles rising, and her mother watching.
A brinjal plant tipped out on newspaper, the root ball white at the top and brown and slimy at the bottom, with a grandmother, a father and a girl looking on.
A new bright green leaf opening at the top of a brinjal plant in a clean pot on two small bricks, and a girl and her grandmother smiling.

games.title: Underground Market: trees and fungi trade for eight rounds
games.players: with a parent or with friends (2 to 4 players: one is the fungus, the others are trees)
games.context: This is a trading game. The trees make sugar but need minerals. The fungus finds minerals but needs sugar. Each side can grow only if they trade.

setup.art: A table with a tree player on one side holding yellow sugar tokens and a fungus player on the other side holding green, red and blue mineral tokens.
setup.caption: 1. The tree holds the sugar tokens. The fungus holds the mineral tokens.

setup.art: Two small decks of cards face down: a SKY deck with a sun on the back and a SOIL deck with a brown clod on the back.
setup.caption: 2. Shuffle the SKY deck and the SOIL deck. Put them face down.

setup.art: A tree and a fungus swapping tokens across the table, a small paper branch and a small paper mushroom beside them.
setup.caption: 3. Trade tokens to build branches and mushrooms.

printables.title: 8 SKY cards: what the weather gives the trees, with the reason on the back

items.f: BRIGHT SUN. Every tree takes 3 sugar tokens.
items.b: Strong light makes photosynthesis fast, so the leaves make a lot of sugar.

items.f: BRIGHT SUN. Every tree takes 3 sugar tokens.
items.b: Strong light makes photosynthesis fast, so the leaves make a lot of sugar.

items.f: BRIGHT SUN. Every tree takes 3 sugar tokens.
items.b: Strong light makes photosynthesis fast, so the leaves make a lot of sugar.

items.f: CLOUDY. Every tree takes 1 sugar token.
items.b: Dim light means slow photosynthesis, so only a little sugar is made.

items.f: CLOUDY. Every tree takes 1 sugar token.
items.b: Dim light means slow photosynthesis, so only a little sugar is made.

items.f: GOOD RAIN. Every tree takes 2 sugar tokens.
items.b: Water is no longer short, and there is enough light, so the leaves make a fair amount of sugar.

items.f: HOT DRY SPELL. Every tree takes 2 sugar tokens. The fungus pays 1 mineral token of their choice to the pile.
items.b: In dry soil, the fungus has to work hard to find water and minerals, and the plant closes the stomata to save water.

items.f: STORM. Every tree takes 0 sugar tokens and loses 1 sugar token they hold.
items.b: A dark storm cuts the light, and wind damages the leaves.

printables.title: 8 SOIL cards: what the fungus finds in the soil, with the reason on the back

items.f: PHOSPHORUS PATCH. The fungus takes 3 phosphorus tokens (red).
items.b: Phosphorus does not move easily through soil, so a root runs out of it close by. The fungus threads reach farther.

items.f: PHOSPHORUS PATCH. The fungus takes 2 phosphorus tokens (red).
items.b: Phosphorus does not move easily through soil, so a root runs out of it close by. The fungus threads reach farther.

items.f: DEAD LEAVES. The fungus takes 2 nitrogen tokens (green).
items.b: Rotting leaves release nitrate, which roots can take in.

items.f: COW DUNG. The fungus takes 2 nitrogen tokens (green) and 1 potassium token (blue).
items.b: Cow dung is a manure. As it rots, it releases nitrogen and potassium.

items.f: WOOD ASH. The fungus takes 3 potassium tokens (blue).
items.b: Wood ash is rich in potassium and some other minerals that the tree took from the soil.

items.f: COMPOST. The fungus takes 1 nitrogen, 1 phosphorus and 1 potassium token.
items.b: Compost holds a little of each mineral, and it keeps the soil loose, with gaps for air.

items.f: WATERLOGGED CORNER. The fungus takes nothing and everyone pays 1 sugar token.
items.b: When water fills all the gaps, the roots and fungus run short of oxygen and cannot take in anything.

items.f: ROCKY GROUND. The fungus takes 1 phosphorus token (red).
items.b: Stony ground holds few minerals, but the fungus can still find a little in the gaps between the stones.

printables.title: Tokens and pieces to make at home
items: SUGAR: cut about 40 small yellow paper squares, or use 40 yellow beads.
NITROGEN: cut about 12 green paper squares.
PHOSPHORUS: cut about 12 red paper squares.
POTASSIUM: cut about 12 blue paper squares.
BRANCH: draw and cut a small tree branch for each tree player to put on the score sheet.
MUSHROOM: draw and cut a small mushroom for the fungus player.

printables.title: Market scores
items: Round number and the SKY card
Round number and the SOIL card
Who traded the most, and who grew the most?

rules: One player is the fungus. Every other player is a tree. With 2 players, the child can be the tree and the parent the fungus, or the other way round.

Each tree starts with 2 sugar tokens. The fungus starts with 1 nitrogen, 1 phosphorus and 1 potassium token. If there is only one tree, that tree takes 1 extra sugar from every SKY card, except STORM.
Each round has four parts. First, a tree turns over a SKY card, and every tree takes the sugar on it. Second, the fungus turns over a SOIL card and takes the tokens on it.
Third, trees and the fungus can trade. Any tokens can be swapped in any amounts, if both sides agree. A player may say no.
Fourth, building. A tree can build a BRANCH for 2 sugar, 1 nitrogen, 1 phosphorus and 1 potassium. The fungus can build a MUSHROOM for 3 sugar.

At the end of every round, each tree pays 1 sugar to stay alive. This is respiration. The fungus pays 1 sugar only at the end of rounds 2, 4, 6 and 8, because the fungus's thin threads need less. A player who cannot pay loses a branch or a mushroom.
After 8 rounds, add up the branches and mushrooms. If both the trees and the fungus built something, everyone wins together. If only one side built something, talk about why the other side could not.
Both sides can see everything on the table. Talk about what you need and what you can give.

flow.do: Choose who is the fungus. Give each tree 2 sugar tokens and the fungus 1 of each mineral. Shuffle the two decks face down.
flow.say: One of us is the fungus and the rest are trees. The trees make sugar. The fungus finds minerals. Can either side grow alone?
flow.kid: One player is the fungus. The others are trees. Take your tokens.

ask.q: Do you think a tree can build a branch without the fungus? Why?
good: No, because the tree needs minerals.
Yes, because the tree has sugar.
Only if the tree has some minerals already.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Write it on the score sheet and check at the end.
flow.context: This is the first step of Underground Market. You set up the roles.

flow.do: Play rounds 1 and 2. In each round, turn a SKY card, turn a SOIL card, trade and build. Then pay sugar to stay alive.
flow.say: Turn the SKY card first. Trees take sugar. Then the SOIL card. The fungus takes minerals. Then you can trade.
flow.kid: Turn the sky card. Turn the soil card. Trade tokens. Build if you can.

ask.q: What did the fungus have that the trees needed? What did the trees have that the fungus needed?
good: The fungus had minerals. The trees had sugar.
The trees needed phosphorus and nitrogen.
The fungus needed sugar to build mushrooms.

check.q: In the game, each tree pays 1 sugar at the end of every round. What does this stand for?
options: Respiration, which every living being does all the time
check.why: Every living cell burns sugar for energy all the time. In the game, paying 1 sugar each round stands for that. Trees do it too, even in the dark.

flow.context: In this step you play the first two rounds and see what each side has and needs.

flow.do: Play rounds 3 to 5. Keep trading. Write the trades on the score sheet. Notice which SOIL card helps the least.
flow.say: Keep going. What is the fairest trade you can make? Does any card spoil the round for everyone?
flow.kid: Play three more rounds. Write down your trades.

ask.q: What happened when the waterlogged corner came up?
good: The fungus found nothing and everyone paid sugar.
Water filled the gaps and there was no air.
Nobody could build.

flow.parent: If the WATERLOGGED CORNER card has not come up, mention that it is in the pile. When it does come up, ask what it means for the roots in the soil.
flow.context: In this step you play more rounds and see how bad soil changes the trade.

flow.do: Play rounds 6 to 8. Then count the branches and mushrooms.
flow.say: These are the last rounds. After round 8, count the branches and the mushrooms. Who grew?
flow.kid: Play the last three rounds. Count the branches and mushrooms.
flow.parent: If the trees and the fungus did not trade, nobody could build. That is a real result too. Play again and try trading from the start.
flow.context: In this step you finish the game and count what each side built.

flow.do: Read the score sheet together. Compare the game with what happens in a real forest.
flow.say: Did anyone grow without trading? What does this game suggest about trees and the fungi on their roots?
flow.kid: Did anyone grow without trading? What does that show?

ask.q: In the game, the tree gave sugar to the fungus. Why would a tree do that?
good: Because the fungus brings minerals the tree needs.
It is a trade where both gain.
The tree cannot get enough phosphorus alone.

flow.think: Scientists agree that trees and fungi trade. They disagree about how much trees share with each other. How could you test that?
flow.context: This step connects the game to real trees and fungi.

games.title: Plant Doctor: read the clues and find the problem
games.players: alone, with a parent or with friends (1 to 4 players)
games.context: This is a detective game. Each card describes a sick plant. You read the clues and choose what is wrong. Then you check the back.

setup.art: Sixteen patient cards in a pile on a table and seven diagnosis tokens in a row in front of a child.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and the seven diagnosis tokens. Put the cards in a pile.

setup.art: A child reading a card about a yellow-leafed lemon plant and placing one diagnosis token on the table.
setup.caption: 2. Read a case. Put down the diagnosis token that you think fits.

setup.art: The back of the card read aloud, with a tick or a cross and a score pad.
setup.caption: 3. Read the back. Score 2 for a right diagnosis.

printables.title: 16 patient cards: the clues on the front, and the diagnosis and the reason on the back

items.f: A curry leaf plant in Mysuru. The oldest, lowest leaves are turning pale yellow and falling. The new leaves at the top are small and light green. The soil is damp but not soaked, and the plant gets plenty of sun.
items.b: Short of nitrogen. Nitrogen moves from old leaves to feed the new growth, so the oldest leaves yellow first. The soil is not waterlogged and the light is fine.

items.f: A lemon tree in a pot in Madurai. The newest leaves at the tips are pale yellow, but their veins stay green. The old leaves are dark green. The pot drains well.
items.b: Short of iron. Iron cannot move from old leaves to new ones, so the new leaves are the ones that suffer. The veins stay green while the leaf between them goes pale.

items.f: A chilli plant on a balcony in Hyderabad. All the leaves droop. The soil is soaked three fingers deep, the saucer is full, and the soil smells sour. The plant has not been without water for days.
items.b: The roots have no air. The gaps are full of water, so the roots cannot breathe and cannot take up water. The drooping is not thirst.

items.f: A rose in a pot in Pune. A big dose of fertiliser was added yesterday. Today, the leaf edges are brown and crispy, and the leaves look scorched. The soil is a little dry.
items.b: Too much fertiliser. Strong fertiliser salts pull water from the roots, so the leaf edges burn. The fix is to flush the pot with plenty of water and wait.

items.f: A tulsi plant at a window in Chennai. The soil is dry and cracked three fingers deep. The leaves are limp but green, and they perk up an hour after watering.
items.b: Too little water. The plant recovers quickly after watering, so the roots are healthy and the soil was simply dry.

items.f: A moong seedling, grown in a dark cupboard, is tall, thin and pale yellow. The seedling leans towards the crack of light at the door.
items.b: Too little light. A plant in the dark makes no chlorophyll, and stretches to find light.

items.f: A tomato plant in Nashik. The lowest leaves are pale yellow from the tip, and the stems are thin. The soil is loose and well drained, and the plant has had no fertiliser for months.
items.b: Short of nitrogen. The oldest leaves yellow first, and the growth is thin. The soil is not waterlogged and the plant has had no fertiliser.

items.f: A banana plant in Kochi. The leaves are yellow and drooping after a week of heavy rain. The pot has no hole, and there is a puddle on top of the soil.
items.b: The roots have no air. Heavy rain and no drainage filled all the gaps. Without a hole, the water cannot leave.

items.f: A potted jasmine in Kolkata. Leaves are crisp and brown at the edges. The gardener gave double the dose of liquid fertiliser every week for a month. The soil is damp.
items.b: Too much fertiliser. Fertiliser salts build up in a pot with nowhere to go, and burn the roots and leaf edges.

items.f: A money plant on a high shelf in a dim corner in Bengaluru. The stems are long and thin with big gaps between the leaves. The new leaves are small and pale. The soil is damp.
items.b: Too little light. A plant in dim light stretches towards the light, and makes small, pale leaves.

items.f: A new guava seedling in Thrissur, planted in a bright spot. The older leaves are dark green and tinged with purple. Growth is very slow. The soil is a heavy, cold clay.
items.b: Short of phosphorus. Dark green or purple older leaves and slow growth are clues. Cold, heavy soil makes it harder to take up phosphorus.

items.f: A rose cutting in Lucknow. The older leaves have yellow edges that turn brown. The leaves between the edges are green. The plant is in good light and the soil drains well.
items.b: Short of potassium. Potassium moves to new growth, so older leaves show yellow-brown edges first.

items.f: A pot of coriander on a south-facing window in Jaipur. The leaves are pale and wilted every afternoon. The soil is bone dry two fingers deep. The pot is small.
items.b: Too little water. The small pot and strong sun dry the soil quickly. The leaves wilt in the heat of the afternoon.

items.f: A fern in a shady corner in Coorg. The fronds are long, dark green and healthy. The fern is in a dim spot with only a little light.
items.b: Healthy. A fern from the forest floor is made for dim light. Some plants need very little light. Do not move them.

items.f: A potted aloe in a sunny window in Ahmedabad. The fat leaves are soft, mushy and yellow at the base. The pot has no hole, and the plant is watered every day.
items.b: The roots have no air. An aloe stores water in the leaves and likes dry soil. Daily watering with no drainage drowns the roots.

items.f: A bean seedling in a cup of cotton wool in Guwahati. The seedling has been in plain water for two weeks, and is short, with pale green leaves and a thin stem. The seed has shrivelled.
items.b: Short of nitrogen and other minerals. The seed's store ran out, and plain water holds almost no minerals. A few drops of fertiliser would help.

printables.title: Diagnosis tokens to cut out, one set of seven for each player
items: SHORT OF IRON, PHOSPHORUS OR POTASSIUM

rules: Put the cards in a pile, clue side up. Put the seven diagnosis tokens in a row.
Read the top card slowly. The clues tell you which leaves are affected, what the soil is like and what the plant has had.
Choose the diagnosis token you think fits, and put it down. If you are playing with others, everyone chooses and shows at the same time.
Turn the card over and read the back aloud. A right diagnosis scores 2 points. If you can also explain the reason, you score 1 more.
Some cards have more than one problem in the clues. Look for the clue that most strongly points to one cause.
Play all 16 cards, or stop after 8 for a short game. If you are playing alone, try to beat your best score.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and tokens. Put the cards in a pile and the tokens in a row. Read the first card together.
flow.say: You are the plant doctor. Each card describes a sick plant. Read the clues, and choose what is wrong.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. You are the plant doctor.

ask.q: What clues would you look at first on a sick plant?
good: Which leaves are yellow, old or new.
Whether the soil is wet or dry.
How much light the plant gets.

flow.context: This is the first step of Plant Doctor. You set up the cards.

flow.do: Play the first six cards. After each card, read the back aloud and score the points.
flow.say: Read the clues. Put down your diagnosis. Now read the back. Were you right? Why?
flow.kid: Read the clues. Choose a diagnosis. Check the back.

ask.q: Why does a plant with drowned roots look like a plant that is thirsty?
good: Roots with no air cannot take in water, so the leaves droop.
Both have limp leaves.
The roots stop working.

check.q: A plant has pale yellow old leaves, green new leaves and well-drained soil. Which diagnosis is most likely?
check.why: Nitrogen moves from old leaves to new growth, so the old leaves yellow first. Well-drained soil rules out drowned roots, and a plant short of light would stretch.

flow.context: In this step you play the first six cards and learn how to score.

flow.do: Play the next six cards. Notice which clues come up again and again. Keep score.
flow.say: Look for patterns in the clues. Which leaves yellow first? What does the soil feel like? Do you see the same clues again?
flow.kid: Play six more cards. Look for clues that come up again.

ask.q: How can you tell a plant that lacks iron from a plant that lacks nitrogen?
good: Iron shortage shows in the new leaves.
Nitrogen shortage shows in the old leaves.
With iron, the veins stay green.

flow.context: In this step you play more cards and learn to tell similar problems apart.

flow.do: Play the last four cards and add up the scores. Talk about the card that surprised you most.
flow.say: Add up the scores. Which card surprised you most? Did you meet a plant that was fine?
flow.kid: Add up your score. Which card surprised you?
flow.think: A plant cannot say what is wrong. How else do we find out what is wrong with someone who cannot speak?
flow.context: In this step you finish the game and look back at the surprises.

items.p: A plant stands in soaked soil and their leaves droop. What is the best explanation?
opts: The roots have no air, so they cannot take up water
The plant has too much sunlight
The plant is asleep
The soil has run out of water
items.why: Water fills all the gaps and pushes out the air. Roots without oxygen cannot work, so the leaves droop as if the plant were thirsty. A plant in soaked soil does not lack water.

items.p: The air in soil is found in the ____ between the grains.
items.why: Soil is made of grains with gaps between them. The gaps hold air and water, and roots breathe the air.

items.p: A drooping plant always needs more water.
items.why: False. A plant droops from too little water, and also when the roots are drowning in too much. Feel the soil before you water.

items.p: You pour water onto 100 millilitres of dry soil. 40 millilitres go in before the water reaches the top. What does this show?
opts: About 40 out of every 100 millilitres of the soil were gaps
The soil weighs 40 grams
The soil is 40 per cent water
Only 40 millilitres of the soil is useful
items.why: The water filled the gaps and pushed the air out. So the water that went in equals the gaps that were there. 40 out of 100 were gaps.
items.context: In the Soil Breath test, you pour water onto 100 millilitres of dry soil until the water reaches the top.

items.p: Each line describes nitrogen, phosphorus or potassium. Sort them.
items: Needed to make chlorophyll and proteins
Needed to build energy carriers and DNA
Helps the stomata open and close
Old leaves turn pale yellow when it is short
Dark green or purple leaves and slow growth when it is short
Older leaves get yellow-brown edges when it is short
items.a: see items
items.why: Nitrogen builds chlorophyll and proteins, phosphorus builds energy carriers and DNA, and potassium helps manage water and the stomata. Each shortage leaves its own clue.

items.p: A path that people walk on every day has few plants. What is the best reason?
opts: Walking packs the soil, squeezing the gaps so roots get little air
People take the minerals away on their feet
Soil on paths is always poisonous
Plants dislike the sound of walking
items.why: Packed soil has fewer and smaller gaps, so there is less air for roots. In the Soil Breath test, packed soil took in less water than loose soil.

items.p: Match each clue to the most likely problem.
pairs: Pale old leaves, green new leaves, well-drained soil
Short of nitrogen
New leaves yellow with green veins
Short of iron
Brown, crispy leaf edges the day after a big dose of fertiliser
Too much fertiliser
Drooping leaves and soaked, sour-smelling soil
Roots have no air
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Where the yellowing starts, and what the soil is like, point to the cause. Nitrogen moves to new growth, so old leaves yellow first. Iron cannot move, so new leaves show it.

items.p: Put these steps in order to show how a plant in soaked soil gets sick.
items: Water fills all the gaps in the soil
The air is pushed out of the gaps
The roots run out of oxygen
The roots cannot take up water or minerals
The leaves droop and turn yellow
items.a: order shown
items.why: Each step causes the next. The drooping leaves are the last sign, not the first. The trouble starts underground.

items.p: Plants cannot use the nitrogen gas in the air directly.
items.why: True. Nitrogen gas has its atoms locked together very tightly. Plants need nitrogen that has been fixed, such as nitrate in the soil.

items.p: A farmer grows black gram after a crop of rice in the same field. What is the farmer making use of?
opts: Bacteria in the dal's roots that put nitrogen into the soil
A way of making the soil harder
A way of scaring away insects
A way of drying the soil
items.why: Rice takes nitrogen out of the soil. A legume such as black gram has root nodules with bacteria that fix nitrogen from the air, and leaves some for the next crop.

items.p: A bean plant gives sugar to the bacteria in their root nodules. In return, the bacteria give the plant ____.
items.why: The bacteria turn nitrogen gas from the air into a form the plant can use. Both sides gain from the trade.

items.p: A friend's tulsi is drooping, and the soil is wet three knuckles deep. Your friend wants to water the plant again. What would you say, and why?
items.a: A strong answer says not to water the plant. Drooping in wet soil can mean the roots are drowning. The wet soil has no air in its gaps, so the roots cannot breathe or take up water. Check that the pot drains, empty the saucer, and wait until the soil is dry two knuckles deep before watering.
items.why: The answer should use the idea that roots need air, and should offer a check or a fix.

items.p: A plant has plenty of phosphorus and potassium but very little nitrogen. Using the idea of the barrel with planks of different heights, explain why more potassium will not help.
items.a: A strong answer says that the plant grows only as well as the shortest supply allows, like water in a barrel only filling to the shortest plank. Nitrogen is the shortest plank. Adding potassium raises a plank that is already tall, so nothing changes until nitrogen is supplied.
items.why: The answer should name nitrogen as the limit and say why adding another mineral changes nothing.

items.p: Draw a cutaway of a pot with soil grains, gaps and one root. Colour the air in the gaps one colour and water in the gaps another colour.
items.a: Brown round grains with gaps between them, a root with root hairs running through the gaps, the air gaps in one colour and the water gaps in another, and a hole at the bottom of the pot.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that some gaps hold air and some hold water, and that the root lives in the gaps.
items.art: An empty outline of a flowerpot with room for soil, a root and labels.

items.p: A grandmother in Kochi, her grandson Kabir and a neighbour argue about a banana plant with yellow, drooping leaves in a pot with no hole.

views.says: She is thirsty. Give her two mugs of water every day.
Check the soil first. If it is soaked, the roots may be drowning, and she needs a hole in the pot.
She needs plant food. Put a big spoon of fertiliser in the pot.

items.ask: Whose advice would you follow first? Use what you know about roots and air. Then say one fair point for someone you disagree with.
items.a: Any choice can be strong if it uses the science. A strong answer follows Kabir: check the soil, and if it is soaked, drain it, because roots need air. It gives Meenakshi credit that a dry plant does droop, and Hari credit that a plant may need minerals later. But more water or fertiliser on drowned roots makes things worse.
items.why: Kabir's advice checks the cause before acting. Water and fertiliser would not help roots that have no air. The other views are reasonable guesses, but they come before the facts.

items.p: Which is the most useful first check for a drooping plant in a pot?
opts: Push a finger into the soil and feel whether it is wet or dry, and check the drain hole
Add fertiliser at once
Move the plant into a dark cupboard
Water the plant again just in case
items.why: The soil tells you whether the problem is too little water or too much. The drain hole tells you whether water can get out. Acting before checking can make a drowning plant worse.

worksheets.title: Minerals, Partners and the Shortest Plank (stretch)

items.p: Bean seedlings grew in three jars. Jar A had plain water and the seedlings were pale and small. Jar B had a small dose of fertiliser and the seedlings were green and tall. Jar C had a big dose and the seedlings were short with brown root tips. What does the difference between B and C show?
opts: More fertiliser is not always better, because too much can harm roots
More fertiliser is always better
Fertiliser has no effect
Brown tips mean the roots are healthy
items.why: A small dose gave the best growth, and a large dose harmed the roots. A plant needs minerals, but a strong dose of salts can scorch the roots. The plain water jar shows that the seedlings do need minerals.
items.context: In the Seedlings Without Soil test, you grow bean seedlings in plain water, a small dose of fertiliser and a big dose.

items.p: Why can a plant surrounded by air still be short of nitrogen?
opts: The atoms in nitrogen gas are locked together, and the plant cannot use the gas until it is fixed
There is no nitrogen in air
Plants breathe only oxygen
Nitrogen is poisonous to plants
items.why: About 78 parts in 100 of the air is nitrogen gas. Its atoms are joined too strongly for a plant to use. Bacteria, lightning and factories must first fix it into forms such as nitrate.

items.p: Fixing nitrogen means joining nitrogen from the ____ to other atoms, so that plants can use it.
items.why: Nitrogen gas in the air is turned into nitrate or ammonium. Bacteria, lightning and factories can all do it.

items.p: Plants grown with their roots in water holding only a few mineral salts, and no soil, can grow well and make seeds.
items.why: True. Julius Sachs and Wilhelm Knop showed this around 1860. The plant makes their own food from carbon dioxide and water, and takes in only minerals and water through the roots.

items.p: A plant has plenty of nitrogen and potassium but very little phosphorus. A farmer adds a lot more nitrogen. What does the shortest plank idea predict?
opts: Little change, because phosphorus is still the shortest supply
The plant will grow twice as fast
The plant will make their own phosphorus
The plant will stop needing phosphorus
items.why: Growth is held back by the shortest supply. Adding more of a mineral that is already plentiful does not help until the limiting one is supplied.

items.p: Match each partnership to what each side gives.
pairs: Legume and root bacteria
The plant gives sugar and the bacteria give nitrogen
Tree and root fungus
The plant gives sugar and the fungus gives water and phosphorus
Azolla and the bacteria in the leaves
The fern gives a home and the bacteria give nitrogen
Compost heap and decomposers
The dead plants give food and the decomposers give back minerals
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: In each partnership, both sides get something. This kind of trade between different living things is very common.

items.p: Which sentence describes mycorrhiza best?
