opts: A fungus and a plant root work together, and the plant gives sugar in return for minerals and water
A fungus that kills the plant's roots
A root that eats insects
A mushroom that grows on dead wood
items.why: Mycorrhiza means fungus root. The fungus threads reach farther into the soil than roots can, and the plant pays with sugar. The partnership helps both sides.

items.p: Sort these statements by whether scientists agree on them or still argue.
items: Most land plants have fungi on their roots
Old mother trees feed their young on purpose through fungus networks
Whether the Green Revolution was good overall
items.a: see items
items.why: Some findings come from many repeat tests. Others depend on how we weigh evidence or what we mean by a word. Good scientists keep the two apart.

items.p: Put these in order to show nitrogen's trip from a bean to the next crop.
items: Bacteria in the bean's root nodules fix nitrogen from the air
The bean plant uses it to build leaves and seeds
The bean plant is harvested and the roots are left in the soil
Decomposers release nitrate from the dead roots
The next rice crop takes in the nitrate
items.a: order shown
items.why: The nitrogen goes from the air into the bean, then back into the soil, and then into the next crop. This is why farmers grow dal in turns with cereals.

items.p: A farmer says, 'The plant's food is in the fertiliser bag.' Explain what is right and what is missing.
items.a: A strong answer says that fertiliser gives minerals such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, which a plant needs to build leaves, roots and seeds. But a plant's food, the sugar, is made in the leaves by photosynthesis from carbon dioxide and water, using light. Minerals are needed like vitamins and building parts. Without the sugar, the minerals cannot be used.
items.why: The answer should separate the minerals from the food, and say where the food is made.

items.p: A tree sends sugar down to a fungus on their roots. Explain why the tree does this, and what the tree gets back.
items.a: A strong answer says the fungus threads reach farther and into smaller gaps than the root, so they bring water and minerals, especially phosphorus, that the tree could not reach alone. The tree pays with some of the sugar made in the leaves. Both gain.
items.why: The answer should state the exchange, and say why each side needs the other.

items.p: Draw the root of a bean plant with nodules. Show the bacteria and add arrows for sugar and nitrogen.
items.a: A root with small round lumps, one cut open to show bacteria inside, an arrow of sugar going from the plant into the nodule, and an arrow of nitrogen going from the nodule into the plant.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the trade in both directions.
items.art: An empty root outline with room for nodules and arrows.

items.p: Carl Sprengel described the shortest plank idea before Justus von Liebig made it famous.
items.why: True. Sprengel wrote about it in 1828, and Liebig made it famous in the 1840s. Some scientists now say it should be called the Sprengel-Liebig law.

items.p: Why did the chemistry of Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch matter for feeding people?
opts: It let factories fix nitrogen from the air into fertiliser on a huge scale
It made soil from rock
It taught plants to fix their own nitrogen
It made rain
items.why: Before the early 1900s, nitrogen for crops came from manure, legumes and a few mineral deposits. Factory ammonia gave much more. It is estimated to feed roughly half the people alive today.

items.p: Three people argue about organic and factory fertiliser.

views.says: Compost and manure feed the soil life and keep the soil loose. We should use them.
The plant takes up the same simple minerals from either. Use what the crop needs, and use both wisely.

views.who: Sunita, a farmer with a big field
views.says: I cannot find enough manure for all my land. Factory fertiliser lets me feed my family.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Use what you know about minerals and soil. Then say one fair point from someone you disagree with.
items.a: Any choice can be strong. A strong answer notes that a root takes up the same simple minerals from either kind, but that manure and compost also open the soil and feed soil life, while factory fertiliser is quick and exact. It gives Sunita credit that supply and cost are real limits, or Lakshmi credit for looking after the soil over many years.
items.why: Each view has a real point. The science says the minerals are the same, but the effects on soil structure, cost and run-off are different. There is no single right answer.

items.p: In 2023, a group of scientists reviewed the studies on fungus networks in forests. They said that some popular claims go beyond the evidence. What does this show about science?
opts: Scientists check each other's claims, and claims should match the evidence
Science is always wrong
Popular books are always right
Fungus networks do not exist
items.why: The reviewers did not say that fungus networks do not exist. They said that some claims were stronger than the studies. Checking and correcting is how science works.

items.p: Here are the results for three soils in the Soil Breath test. Which soil has the most room for air for roots to breathe?
opts: Loose garden soil
Sand
Packed garden soil
They all have exactly the same
items.why: The bar for loose garden soil is the tallest, at 44. Packed soil has the smallest. Packing squeezes the gaps, so there is less air for roots.
items.context: In the Soil Breath test, you measure how many millilitres of water fill the gaps in 100 millilitres of soil. These are made-up results.

items.p: In the Soil Breath test, you measure the water that goes in, but you say you have measured the air. Why is that fair?
opts: The water fills the gaps and pushes the air out, so the water equals the air that was there
Water and air are the same thing
The air is heavier than water
The air turns into water in the soil
items.why: The water can only go where the air was. When the water reaches the top, it has taken the place of all the air in the gaps. So the volume of water equals the volume of gaps.

items.p: A 50-kilogram bag of fertiliser is labelled 20-10-10, which gives the percentages of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. About ____ kilograms of the bag are nitrogen.
items.why: 20 per cent of 50 kilograms is 10 kilograms, because 50 divided by 5 is 10. The rest of the bag is other things.

items.p: A leaf that turns yellow always means the plant is short of a mineral.
items.why: False. Yellow leaves can come from drowned roots, too little light, a shortage of nitrogen or iron, and more. A plant doctor checks the soil and the roots, too.

items.p: Match each plant to the way they cope with their roots or their soil.
pairs: Rice
Air channels carry air from the leaves to the roots in mud
Mangrove
Pencil-like roots stick up out of the mud to breathe
Groundnut
Nodules on the roots hold nitrogen-fixing bacteria
A forest tree
Fungus threads help gather phosphorus and water
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each plant has their own solution. Rice and mangrove solve the problem of no air in mud. The groundnut solves the problem of low nitrogen. The tree uses help from fungi.

items.p: The saucer under a pot plant has been full of water for a week, and the leaves are yellow. What is the best first action?
opts: Empty the saucer, check the drain hole and let the soil dry a little before watering
Add a spoon of fertiliser
Water the plant more
Cover the pot with a plastic bag
items.why: The roots are probably short of air. Letting the water drain and the soil dry a little brings air back into the gaps. Fertiliser or more water would make the problem worse.

items.p: Farms that grow lettuce with their roots in flowing water often pump air bubbles into the water. Why?
opts: Roots in water still need oxygen to breathe
The bubbles feed the lettuce
The bubbles keep the water cold
The bubbles make the lettuce taste sweeter
items.why: Root cells respire, and they need dissolved oxygen. Still water can run short of oxygen. Air bubbles keep it supplied.

items.p: Sort each farming practice by what it does to the nitrogen in the soil.
items: Ploughing in a green manure plant such as dhaincha
items.a: see items
items.why: Legumes and compost put nitrogen into the soil. Cereal crops take it out and carry it away in the grain.

items.p: Put these in order to show how kitchen peels turn into plant food.
items: Peels and dry leaves are mixed in a heap
Bacteria and fungi start to rot them
The heap shrinks and turns dark
The humus releases minerals to a plant's roots
items.a: order shown
items.why: Decomposers break the peels down. What is left is humus, which holds water and releases minerals to roots over time.
items.context: In the compost bottle project, you turn kitchen peels and dry leaves into compost over five weeks.

items.p: Design a fair test to find out whether radish seedlings grow better in compost than in plain sand. Say what you keep the same, what you change and what you measure.
items.a: A strong answer uses two pots of the same size, the same number of seeds, the same water and the same light. The only change is the material: compost in one and plain sand in the other. It measures the height of the seedlings and the colour of the leaves after two weeks. It repeats the test or uses several seeds, because one seed could be a fluke.
items.why: The answer should keep everything the same except one thing, and say what will be measured.

items.p: A neighbour says, 'Roots are just pipes for water.' Give two pieces of evidence from this unit that roots are alive and need air.
items.a: A strong answer gives two pieces of evidence. First, roots drown in waterlogged soil even though water is plentiful, because they need oxygen. Second, cuttings grow fewer roots in water with the air boiled out, and seedlings in water need an air gap. Or: bubbles of air come out of soil when you pour water on it, and the root lives in those gaps.
items.why: The answer should give evidence from tests or observations, and link it to roots respiring.

items.p: Explain why a plant short of iron shows yellow new leaves, but a plant short of nitrogen shows yellow old leaves.
items.a: A strong answer says that nitrogen can be moved around inside the plant, so a plant short of it takes nitrogen out of the old leaves and sends it to the new growth, so the old leaves turn yellow first. Iron cannot be moved once it is in a leaf, so new leaves, which have no iron stored, show the shortage first.
items.why: The answer should say that the difference comes from whether the mineral can move within the plant.

items.p: Draw a barrel with five planks labelled N, P, K, Ca and Fe, where nitrogen is the shortest. Draw what happens when a farmer adds potassium. Then draw what happens when she adds nitrogen.
items.a: A barrel with the N plank shortest. After adding potassium the K plank is no different and the water level is still at N. After adding nitrogen the N plank is lengthened, and the water rises to the next shortest plank.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the level stays at the shortest plank until that plank is fixed, and then moves to the next.
items.art: An empty barrel outline with space for five planks.

items.p: Three people discuss the Green Revolution in India.

views.says: New short wheat and rice, fertiliser and irrigation saved millions of people from hunger. We would not have enough food without them.
My borewell has dried up, I owe money for seed and fertiliser, and my soil is tired.

views.who: Anbu, a researcher who studies millets
views.says: We lost many old crops that need less water. We should bring them back alongside the new ones.

items.ask: Which of these views do you find the most convincing? What facts would you want to know? Then say one fair point from someone you disagree with.
items.a: Any choice can be strong. A strong answer uses facts about fertiliser, water and soil, for example that fertiliser raises yields but uses water and money, and that rotating crops and compost might help the soil. It gives each person credit: Dr. Swati for the hunger that was avoided, Harjeet for the real cost, or Anbu for the idea of keeping variety.
items.why: All three views are partly right. The honest answer weighs a large benefit against real costs, and looks for ways to keep the benefit while reducing the costs.

items.p: Scientists found that carbon moved between trees through fungus threads. Which of these conclusions goes beyond that evidence?
opts: Old trees care for their own young on purpose
Carbon can move between trees through fungi
Fungi can link the roots of different trees
Some carbon passes through the fungus
items.why: Three of the statements describe what was measured. The claim that old trees care for their own young on purpose says why the carbon moved. Moving a small amount of carbon does not show that a tree acts on purpose to help their young.

items.p: Roots grow evenly in all directions, whatever is in the soil.
items.why: False. Roots grow towards water and mineral-rich patches, branch more where food is plentiful, and bend away from stones and salt.

items.p: Some scientists say roots think and choose. Others say roots only respond automatically. What do the two groups disagree about?
opts: What to call the roots' clever responses, not whether the roots respond
Whether roots grow at all
Whether roots need water
Whether roots exist
items.why: Both groups agree that roots sense and respond in sophisticated ways. They disagree about whether this deserves words such as thinking and choosing.

experiments.title: Soil Breath: how much air is hiding in soil?
experiments.question: Soil looks solid. If you pour water onto 100 millilitres of dry soil, how much water will it take before the water reaches the top? And does the kind of soil, or packing it down, change the answer?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will the gaps in 100 millilitres of soil hold about 10, 25, 50 or 75 millilitres of water? Will loose or packed soil hold more? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every cup is the same size and holds exactly 100 millilitres of dry soil, filled the same way. You pour water at the same slow speed each time and stop at the same sign: a thin shine of water that stays on top for 30 seconds. Only the kind of soil, or how tightly it is packed, changes. So any difference in the water that went in comes from the soil.
results_table: Bubbles: none, a few or lots

materials.item: 3 identical clear cups with straight sides, each holding about 250 millilitres
a measuring jug marked in millilitres, or one spoon used for every measure (a level tablespoon is about 15 millilitres, but household spoons vary)

about 400 millilitres of dry garden soil, crumbled, with no lumps or stones. In monsoon or damp weather, spread it on a newspaper in the sun or under a fan for a day first. Loose potting mix with coir or peat behaves differently, so label it if you use it
about 200 millilitres of dry sand, or dry red soil, as a second kind of soil
a spoon, a marker, a tray and some newspaper (a second spoon or a kitchen cup to pack the soil)
a pot of water and a notebook

experiments.safety: Do not breathe in dry soil dust. Spoon it gently and do not blow on it. Wash hands afterwards.
experiments.record: For each cup, write the water that went in and the percentage of gaps. Write whether the soil was loose or packed. Draw one cup with its bubbles.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you pour water onto dry soil and find out how much of the soil is gaps filled with air. This is the air that roots breathe.

setup.art: A clear cup with a marker line at the 100 millilitre level, and a jug of water being poured into it to check the line.
setup.caption: 1. Mark a line on a cup at 100 millilitres. Pour out the water and dry the cup.

setup.art: Dry soil being spooned into the cup to the line and tapped twice on the table.
setup.caption: 2. Fill the cup with dry soil to the line. Tap it twice.

setup.art: Water poured slowly from a jug onto the soil, with silver bubbles rising up through the soil and a shine of water just reaching the top.
setup.caption: 3. Pour water slowly. Watch the bubbles. Stop when a shine of water reaches the top.

setup.art: A second cup of soil pressed down hard with the back of a spoon, then topped up with more soil to the line.
setup.caption: 4. Pack a second cup of soil down hard, and top it up to the line. Test it the same way.

flow.do: Show the soil, the cup and the water. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: Here is 100 millilitres of dry soil. We will pour water on it until the water just reaches the top. How much water will go in? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Here is dry soil in a cup. How much water will go in before it reaches the top? Why?

ask.q: Where do you think the water will go?
good: Into the soil, between the bits.
It will soak in.
The soil will swell.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Most children guess a small amount, such as 10 to 25 millilitres. With one child, the child pours and watches, and the parent reads the jug. With two to four children, give each child one cup, let the parent read the jug, and compare the numbers on the board.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Soil Breath test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Pour 100 millilitres of water into a clear cup and mark the level with a marker. Pour the water out and dry the cup. Make two more cups the same way.
flow.say: Measure 100 millilitres of water into a cup. Mark where it reaches. Pour it out and dry the cup. Do that for all three cups.
flow.kid: Fill a cup with 100 millilitres of water. Mark the line. Pour it out.
flow.parent: If you have no measuring jug, count tablespoons. Seven level tablespoons is about 100 millilitres. Spoons vary, so use the same spoon every time. If your spoon is not 15 millilitres, count how many spoonfuls fill the cup to the line. Later, compare the spoonfuls of water that go into the soil with that number. The three cups must be the same size and shape.

check.q: Why do we mark all three cups at exactly 100 millilitres?
options: So that each cup holds the same amount of soil
So that the cups look neat
So that the water is cold
So that the bubbles are bigger
check.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. If one cup held more soil, it could take more water for that reason, and not because of the kind of soil.

flow.context: In this step, you mark three cups so that each holds exactly 100 millilitres of soil.

flow.do: Fill cup one with dry garden soil to the line. Tap the cup twice. Pour water from the jug slowly. Stop when a shine of water shows at the top. Write down how much you used.
flow.say: Pour slowly, a little at a time. Watch for bubbles. Stop when you see a shine of water on top. How much did you pour in?
flow.kid: Pour water slowly onto the soil. Watch the bubbles. Stop at the shine.

ask.q: What are the bubbles? Where did they come from?
good: Air that was in the soil.
The air was between the bits of soil.
The water pushed the air out.

flow.parent: Read the amount from the jug: the water you started with minus the water left. Garden soil usually takes about 35 to 50 millilitres, but your soil may differ, and a jug is only accurate to about 5 to 10 millilitres. Pour a little, wait for it to sink in, then pour more. The soil may need a minute to soak, and the last bit needs patience. If water sits on top at once and will not sink, crumble the soil finer and try again. With more than one child, each child tests one cup. Then they swap and repeat the same test to see if they get the same number. Write down any result as it is.

check.q: The cup holds 100 millilitres of soil, and 45 millilitres of water went in before it reached the top. What does the 45 millilitres tell you?
options: About 45 out of every 100 millilitres of the soil was gaps filled with air
The water is 45 per cent soil
check.why: The water went into the gaps and pushed the air out as bubbles. The amount of water that went in equals the amount of gaps. So about 45 out of 100 of the soil was gaps.

flow.context: In this step, you pour water on the first cup and measure the gaps.

flow.do: Repeat with sand or red soil in cup two. Then fill cup three with garden soil, press it hard with a spoon, top up to the line, and test it.
flow.say: Test the second soil the same way. Then pack the third cup down hard and top it up to the line. Which takes less water?
flow.kid: Test the sand. Then pack a cup of soil hard and test it.

ask.q: Why does packed soil take less water?
good: Pressing squeezes the gaps smaller.
There is less air space.
There is more soil and fewer gaps.

flow.parent: Sand usually takes about 30 to 40 millilitres. Packed soil takes a little less than loose soil, often 3 to 10 millilitres less. Packing sand changes it only a little, and that is a real result. If the packed cup gives the same number as the loose one, repeat both and press harder. A gardener's path or a trampled field is like packed soil.
flow.context: In this step, you test another soil and a packed soil, and compare them.

flow.do: Write down all the results. Ask your child what they found (the claim), what they saw that shows it (the evidence) and why it happens (the reasoning). Draw one cup with its bubbles.
flow.say: What did you find? What did you see that shows it? Why does that matter for a root in a pot?
flow.kid: What did you find? What did you see? Why does it matter for roots?

ask.q: What would happen to the air in the soil if you filled the gaps with water and left them full?
good: The roots would have no air.
The roots would drown.
The air would be pushed out and the roots could not breathe.

check.q: A pot of soil stays filled with water for many days. What happens to the roots?
options: They run out of air and begin to die
They grow faster because they have more water
check.why: Water in all the gaps leaves no room for air. Roots are alive and need oxygen to respire, so they begin to die, even though there is plenty of water.

flow.think: If the gaps are half of the soil, where are most of a plant's roots living: in the grains, or in the gaps?
flow.context: In this step, you say what you found and link it to the roots of a plant.

experiments.title: Seedlings Without Soil: do plants need minerals?
experiments.question: A seedling can grow with no soil at all. Does a bean seedling need minerals in the water? And is a lot of fertiliser better than a little?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After two weeks, which jar will have the tallest, greenest seedlings? Which will have the smallest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: All three jars are the same size, hold the same amount of the same water, and get the same light. Each has three seedlings of the same age and kind. Only the fertiliser changes: none in jar A, a small dose in jar B and a big dose in jar C. So any difference comes from the fertiliser.
results_table: Jar A (plain water): height and leaf colour
Jar B (a small dose): height and leaf colour
Jar C (a big dose): height and leaf colour

materials.item: 3 clear jars or glasses, each holding about 300 millilitres
9 rajma (kidney bean) seeds, soaked for 6 hours, then sprouted in a damp cloth for 3 days (soak 12 so that you can choose the best 9)
3 squares of thick card or foam, each with 3 holes about 1 centimetre wide, big enough to rest on the jar's mouth
liquid plant fertiliser with a measuring spoon or dropper, a 1-litre bottle and a measuring jug
about 1.5 litres of low-mineral water: rainwater from a clean bowl, RO water, or a bottle of distilled water (sold for steam irons)
a ruler, a marker, tape, dark paper to wrap the jars, green crayons in 4 shades and a notebook

experiments.safety: A grown-up reads the label and measures the fertiliser, because it can irritate eyes and skin. Keep it away from the mouth, and wash hands after touching the jars. Do not drink the water. Raw rajma seeds and sprouts are poisonous if eaten, so do not taste them, and do not cook any of these beans for food.
experiments.record: Counting from the day you soak the seeds, on days 4, 8, 12 and 18, measure the tallest shoot in each jar, match the leaf colour to a crayon, and note any brown or soft roots. Draw the three jars at the end.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you grow bean seedlings with their roots in water, with no soil. You find out if they need minerals, and if more fertiliser is better.

setup.art: Rajma seeds wrapped in a damp cloth on a plate, three days later with white roots and a small shoot.
setup.caption: 1. Sprout rajma seeds in a damp cloth for 3 days.

setup.art: Three jars labelled A, B and C. Jar A has plain water, jar B has half strength fertiliser water and jar C has double strength fertiliser water.
setup.caption: 2. Fill three jars with water. Add fertiliser at half strength to B and at double strength to C.

setup.art: A card square with holes resting on a jar, three bean sprouts with their roots hanging through the holes into the water.
setup.caption: 3. Rest each sprout on a card with their roots hanging in the water.

setup.art: Three jars on a bright windowsill after two to three weeks: the plants in A paler and shorter, those in B greenest and tallest, and those in C smaller than B, perhaps with brown root tips.
setup.caption: 4. After two weeks, compare the three jars.

flow.do: Show the seeds, the jars and the fertiliser. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: We will grow beans with their roots in water, with no soil. One jar has plain water. One has a little fertiliser. One has a lot. Which will grow best? Why?
flow.kid: Beans will grow in water with no soil. One jar has plain water, one has a little fertiliser and one has a lot. Which will grow best? Why?

ask.q: Do you think a bean can grow in plain water? For how long?
good: Yes, because the seed has food stored.
Only for a few days.
No, because plants need soil.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A bean has a food store in the seed, so the seedling can grow for a while in plain water. The question is for how long.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Seedlings Without Soil test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Soak the rajma seeds for 6 hours. Wrap them in a damp cloth. Keep the cloth damp for 3 days, until each seed has a white root 2 to 3 centimetres long.
flow.say: Soak the seeds. Wrap them in a damp cloth. Keep the cloth damp. After three days, you will see white roots.
flow.kid: Soak the beans. Wrap them in a damp cloth. Wait three days.
flow.parent: Sprout a few more than nine seeds, in case some do not sprout. Rinse the cloth once a day with clean water. If a seed turns soft or smells sour, throw that seed away. At the end, choose nine seeds with matching roots.
flow.context: In this step, you sprout the beans so that they have roots.

flow.do: A grown-up reads the fertiliser label and mixes 1 litre of strong solution in the bottle, at double the label dose. Pour 300 millilitres of strong solution into jar C. For jar B, mix 75 millilitres (five tablespoons) of strong solution with 225 millilitres of low-mineral water. Fill jar A with 300 millilitres of low-mineral water only.
flow.say: Jar A gets plain low-mineral water. Jar C gets the strong solution, double the label dose. Jar B gets one quarter of that, which is half the label dose. A grown-up measures. Mark the jars.
flow.kid: A grown-up measures the fertiliser. Mark the jars A, B and C.
flow.parent: Labels usually give a dose per litre, so double it for the strong solution (for example, 2.5 millilitres per litre becomes 5). Measure carefully, because the point of the test is the difference in dose. Ordinary tap water already holds some minerals, so jar A is only low in minerals, not empty, and the difference may be smaller. Wrap each jar in dark paper to stop green slime growing on the roots. Tape the card over each jar and push the sprouts through, so that the seed rests on the card and only the roots reach the water. Leave a small air gap between the water and the card, because roots need air too. Top up with the same solution when the water drops. With one child, the child sets up and measures all three jars. With two to four children, each child takes one jar, and then they compare.

check.q: Why do we leave a small air gap between the water and the card?
options: Roots in water still need air to breathe
check.why: Roots respire and need oxygen. If the whole root were under water in a still jar, the root could run short of oxygen. The air gap, and the water level touching just the lower roots, help the roots breathe.

flow.context: In this step, you make the three solutions and set up the seedlings.

flow.do: On days 4, 8 and 12, measure the tallest shoot in each jar and match the leaf colour. Write the results. Top up the water.
flow.say: Measure the tallest shoot in each jar. Match the leaf colour to a crayon. What is changing? What is the same?
flow.kid: Measure the tallest shoot in each jar. Match the leaf colour.

ask.q: Which jar is doing best so far? Which is doing worst?
good: Jar B is tallest and greenest.
Jar A is pale.
Jar C has brown tips.

flow.parent: Seeds have their own store, so the three jars may look alike for the first week or so. Differences usually start to show in the second or third week, and the full signs can take 2 to 4 weeks. Change all the water and solutions every 5 days, or every 3 days in hot weather, with the same doses. Use a bright window, because in a dim room all three jars stay pale. If a root turns slimy or smells sour, rinse the root and write it down.
flow.context: In this step, you check the seedlings as they grow and write the measurements.

flow.do: On day 18, measure and match the colours again. Check the roots. Draw the three jars. Write what you found (the claim), what you saw that shows it (the evidence) and why it happened (the reasoning).
flow.say: Compare the three jars. Which seedlings look healthiest? What happened to the roots in jar C? What does this show?
flow.kid: Compare the three jars. Check the roots. Which grew best?

ask.q: Why might a big dose of fertiliser be worse than a small dose?
good: Strong fertiliser can burn the roots.
Too many salts make it hard for roots to take in water.
More is not always better.

check.q: Seedlings in plain water are pale and small after two weeks, though the seeds were healthy. What is the best explanation?
options: Plain water has almost no minerals, and the seeds' store has run out
check.why: Water alone gives the plant no nitrogen, phosphorus or potassium. The seed held a small store that lasts a while. When it runs out, the seedling is short of minerals and turns pale.

flow.parent: If all three jars still look alike on day 18, the seeds' store may have lasted. That is a real result too. Leave the jars up to day 28 and measure on days 22 and 28, or repeat with smaller seeds such as moong. Jar C may look as good as jar B, because a houseplant fertiliser at double dose does not always burn roots. That is also a real result: the harm starts at a much stronger dose, which a child should not handle alone.
flow.think: A plant in a field gets minerals from soil where leaves have been rotting for years. What does the soil give that plain water does not?
flow.context: In this step, you compare the three jars at the end and say what minerals do.

schedule.what: Soak the seeds and wrap them in a damp cloth. Keep the cloth damp.
Make the three jars and set up the sprouts. Measure the starting height.
Measure the shoots and match the leaf colours.
Measure again and match the colours. Change the water.
Measure, check the roots and draw the jars. Write what you found, what you saw that shows it, and why it happened.

experiments.title: Roots Need to Breathe: cuttings in boiled water with and without air
experiments.question: A cutting grows new roots in water. Does the water need to have air in it? What happens if you take the air out of the water?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. After ten days, which jar will have more and longer roots: the one with air in the water, or the one with the air shut out? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Both jars hold the same boiled and cooled water, five cuttings each of the same plant, in the same light. Boiling drives most of the dissolved air out of the water. In jar A, a thin layer of oil on top keeps new air from getting in. In jar B, there is no oil, and you stir the water each day so that air mixes in. Only the air in the water changes.
results_table: Number of new roots at day 10
Colour and feel of the roots

materials.item: 2 clear glass jars or tall glasses, each holding about 300 millilitres
2 clear glass jars or tall glasses, each holding about 300 millilitres
10 fresh cuttings of mint (pudina), coleus or tomato, each about 10 centimetres long, cut just below a joint, with the lower leaves removed
700 millilitres of water boiled for 5 minutes by a grown-up, then cooled with a lid on
1 teaspoon of cooking oil and a clean spoon (use sunflower or mustard oil, and avoid groundnut oil if anyone has a nut allergy)

experiments.safety: A grown-up boils the water and lets it cool completely before it is poured. Take care with oil, which makes floors slippery. Do not eat the cuttings from the test. Wash the spoon and jars well afterwards.
experiments.record: On days 3, 6 and 10, count the new roots and measure the longest root in each jar. Draw one cutting from each jar.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you grow cuttings in water that has had its air boiled out, and in water that has air. You find out if roots need to breathe.

setup.art: A pot of water boiling on a stove with a grown-up beside it, then a lid on the pot as it cools.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up boils water for 5 minutes and lets it cool with a lid on.

setup.art: Two jars each with five mint cuttings in boiled water, one with a thin layer of oil on top and one without.
setup.caption: 2. Put five cuttings in each jar. Pour a thin layer of oil on jar A.

setup.art: A child stirring the water in jar B with a spoon while jar A, with oil on top, is left alone.
setup.caption: 3. Each day, stir jar B gently. Leave jar A alone.

setup.art: Two jars after ten days: jar B typically with more and longer white roots, jar A with fewer, shorter or brownish roots.
setup.caption: 4. On day 10 to 12, count and measure the roots.

flow.do: Show the cuttings and the jars. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: Boiling water drives out its air. Oil on top keeps air out. Will roots grow well in water with no air? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One jar has water with no air. The other has water with air. In which jar will roots grow better? Why?

ask.q: Do you think roots need air? How could we find out?
good: Yes, because roots are alive and breathe.
We could grow roots with and without air.
No, because roots are in water, not air.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Roots Need to Breathe test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: A grown-up boils 600 millilitres of water for 5 minutes. Put a lid on the pot and let it cool completely. This takes about 30 minutes.
flow.say: A grown-up boils the water. Put a lid on the pot. Let the water cool all the way. Boiling drives out the air.
flow.kid: A grown-up boils the water. Let it cool with a lid on.
flow.parent: Dissolved air comes out of water when it is heated. If you pour the water into the jars while it is still hot, you risk cracking glass and burning a child. Cool it to room temperature, then use it. Do not pour it from a great height, which mixes air back in.

check.q: Why do we boil the water for this test?
options: Boiling drives out the dissolved air
check.why: Warm water holds less dissolved gas than cold water, and boiling drives out nearly all of it. That leaves water with very little air for the roots.

flow.context: In this step, a grown-up boils the water to drive out the air.

flow.do: Put five cuttings in each jar. Pour in the cooled water gently. Add a thin layer of oil on the top of jar A. Leave both jars in the same bright place.
flow.say: Put five cuttings in each jar. Pour in the water gently. Add the oil to jar A only. Put both jars side by side.
flow.kid: Five cuttings in each jar. Add oil to jar A only.
flow.parent: Cut each cutting just below a joint, and remove the bottom leaves so that none sit in the water. Pour the water slowly down the side of the jar to keep air out. Put the oil in after the cuttings, so that the oil does not coat the stems when you push them in. Stir jar B gently with a clean spoon each day for about 30 seconds, to let air in. Do not touch jar A. With one child, the child sets up both jars and does the daily stir. With two to four children, each child takes one cutting in each jar, labels them with a tag, and measures their own.

check.q: What is the oil layer for?
options: It stops new air from dissolving into the water
check.why: Air dissolves into water from the surface. A layer of oil keeps the air away from the water, so no new air gets in.

flow.context: In this step, you set up the two jars, one with air kept out and one with air mixed in.

flow.do: On days 3, 6 and 10, count the new roots and measure the longest in each jar. Stir jar B each day. Write the results.
flow.say: Count the new roots. Measure the longest. Compare the two jars. Do you see a difference?
flow.kid: Count the roots in each jar. Measure the longest.

ask.q: Which jar has more roots so far? Is that what you expected?
good: Jar B has more roots.
There is no difference yet.
Jar A has fewer and they look brown.

flow.parent: Roots may take 5 to 7 days to show, sooner in hot weather. Mint and coleus root easily even in still water, and a cutting can carry some air down inside the stem, so the difference may be small, or none. That is a real result: say so, and repeat with more cuttings or a plant that roots more slowly. Do not top up jar A, because new water brings in air. If the roots in jar A look brown or soft, or the water smells sour, that is a sign of too little air.
flow.context: In this step, you check the jars and write what you see.

flow.do: Between day 10 and day 12, count and measure the roots one last time. Draw one cutting from each jar. Write what you found (the claim), what you saw that shows it (the evidence) and why it happened (the reasoning).
flow.say: Which jar grew more and longer roots? What does that tell us about roots and air?
flow.kid: Which jar has more roots? What does that tell you about air?

ask.q: What might a rice plant or a lotus do that a mint cutting cannot?
good: They carry air down to their roots through channels in the stem.
They have air tubes.
They live in mud where there is no air.

check.q: Cuttings in water with air grew more roots than cuttings in water with the air kept out. What does this show?
options: Roots grow better when they can get oxygen
check.why: The only difference was the air in the water. The roots with more air grew better, so roots need oxygen. The oil did not poison the roots, because it sat on top of the water and did not touch them.

flow.think: A paddy plant grows in water for months. How might the plant get air to the roots?
flow.context: In this step, you compare the two jars and say what roots need.

schedule.what: A grown-up boils the water. Let it cool. Set up the two jars with cuttings, and add the oil to jar A.
Stir jar B. Count and measure the roots.
Stir jar B. Count and measure the roots.
Count and measure the roots one last time. Draw a cutting from each jar. Write what you found, what you saw that shows it, and why it happened.

activities.title: Soil in a Jar: what is soil made of?

materials.item: a tall clear jar with a lid, about 500 millilitres
about 150 millilitres of garden soil with the stones and twigs picked out
water, enough to fill the jar three-quarters full
a ruler and a marker

schedule.what: Shake soil and water in a jar. Watch it settle for 1 minute, then leave it.
Measure and draw the layers.

activities.record: Draw the jar after 1 minute, after 1 hour and after 1 day. Label the layers and measure each with a ruler.
activities.context: In this activity, you shake soil in water and watch it settle into layers. This shows the different grains that soil is made of.

setup.art: A jar a third full of soil and filled with water, a hand tightening the lid.
setup.caption: 1. Put soil in a jar, fill it with water and close the lid.

setup.art: A child shaking the jar hard, and then the jar on a table with swirling brown water.
setup.caption: 2. Shake the jar hard for 1 minute. Put it on the table.

setup.art: The jar a day later with distinct layers: sand at the bottom, silt above, clay above that, clear water and floating bits of leaf on top.
setup.caption: 3. Look at the jar after 1 minute, 1 hour and 1 day. Mark each layer.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess how many layers the soil will make. Write the guess.
flow.say: We will shake soil in water and wait. How many layers do you think will form? What will each be made of? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: You will shake soil in water. How many layers will you see? Why?

ask.q: Do you think the heavy bits or the light bits will settle first?
good: The heavy bits, like sand.
The big bits.
The light bits float.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. If you want more to compare, use two soils (garden soil and sandy or red soil) in two jars. Two to four children can take one jar each, with soil from different places. Most soils make three layers of mineral grains, with floating bits of dead leaf on top.
flow.context: This is the first step of Soil in a Jar. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Fill the jar one-third with soil. Add water to three-quarters. Close the lid. Shake hard for one minute. Stand the jar still. Draw it after one minute and after one hour.
flow.say: Shake the jar for one whole minute. Put it down and watch. What settles first? Draw the jar now.
flow.kid: Shake the jar for one minute. Put it down. Watch what settles first.

ask.q: What do you see settling at the bottom first? What stays cloudy?
good: Sand falls first.
The fine bits stay in the water.
Leaf bits float on top.

flow.parent: Sand settles in about a minute. Silt settles over an hour or two. Clay can take a day or more and may still cloud the water, so after a day the layers may not be sharp. That is normal. Layer thicknesses depend on your soil. Dark floating bits are humus and leaf. Do not shake the jar again after the first minute.

check.q: Why does sand settle first in the jar?
options: Its grains are bigger and heavier, so they sink faster
Sand is attracted to the bottom of the jar
Sand is the only part of the soil that is solid
check.why: Big, heavy grains sink fast in water and tiny ones sink slowly. So the layers form in order of grain size, with sand at the bottom, then silt, then clay.

flow.context: In this step, you shake the soil and watch it settle.

flow.do: The next day, look at the jar. Measure each layer with a ruler. Draw and label the jar. Talk about where the gaps are and where roots live.
flow.say: Measure each layer. Which is thickest? Where do you think the air gaps are in dry soil? What does this soil have that sand alone would not?
flow.kid: Measure each layer. Which is thickest? Draw the jar.
flow.think: Soil is mostly tiny rock grains with a little dead leaf. Why does a plant grow better in soil than in pure sand?
flow.context: In this step, you measure the layers and think about what soil is.

activities.title: Who Lives in the Soil? A spoonful of life (if you have a garden or a park nearby)

materials.item: a white sheet or tray, a spoon and a magnifying glass (or a phone camera zoomed in)
a handful of leaf litter and soil from under a tree or from a compost heap
a notebook and a pencil

schedule.what: Spread a spoonful of soil and leaf litter on a white sheet. Look for living things. Draw and count them.

activities.record: Draw up to five different creatures. Write how many of each you found, and what you think each one eats.
activities.context: In this activity, you look at a spoonful of leaf litter and soil on a white sheet and find the living things that make soil work.

setup.art: A child using a spoon to scoop soil and dead leaves from under a tree into a tray.
setup.caption: 1. Scoop a spoonful of leaf litter and soil from under a tree.

setup.art: The scoop spread out on a white sheet, with a few tiny creatures moving, and a magnifying glass above.
setup.caption: 2. Spread it on a white sheet. Look with a magnifying glass.

setup.art: A notebook page with drawings of an ant, a mite, a springtail, a small worm and a millipede, each with a tally.
setup.caption: 3. Draw and count what you find. Put the creatures back.

flow.do: Ask your child to guess how many different kinds of living thing will be in one spoonful. Write the guess.
flow.say: We will look at one spoonful of soil. How many different living things do you think we will find? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Here is a spoonful of soil. How many living things will you find? Guess.
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Use a spoon and never your fingers, and stay away from anything that stings or bites. Put every creature back where you found them. If you have no garden, use a park, the soil from under a plant pot, or leaf litter from beneath a tree. In hot dry weather, look under stones, pots or damp leaves. One child can do it alone with a parent watching. Two to four children can take one sheet each, with soil from different spots, and compare.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Lives in the Soil? You guess before you look.

flow.do: Spread the spoonful on the white sheet. Look slowly with the magnifier for five minutes. Draw each kind you find and tally how many.
flow.say: Wait and watch. Some creatures are very small and slow. Draw each kind you find. Count how many of each.
flow.kid: Spread the soil on the sheet. Look with a magnifier. Draw and count.

ask.q: What do you think each creature eats? What do they do in the soil?
good: They eat dead leaves.
They break down the leaves into smaller bits.
Some eat other tiny creatures.

flow.parent: You may find ants, mites, springtails, small worms, beetle grubs and millipedes. Many are decomposers that eat dead leaves. Do not worry if you find few. In a very dry or very sandy soil, you will find less. Try under a damp leaf pile.

check.q: Why are creatures in the soil useful to plants?
options: They break dead leaves into minerals and keep the soil loose
check.why: Soil creatures eat and rot dead leaves, releasing minerals that roots can take in. Their burrows and movement keep the soil loose, with gaps for air.

flow.context: In this step, you look at the spoonful and find the living things.

flow.do: Put the creatures and the soil back gently. Count how many kinds you found. Talk about who does what.
flow.say: Put them back where you found them. How many kinds did you count? Who do you think does the most work?
flow.kid: Put the creatures back. How many kinds did you find?
flow.think: There are more living things in a spoon of healthy soil than you can count. What do they do while we are not looking?
flow.context: In this step, you return the soil and think about who does what.

activities.title: Find the Pink Factories: nodules on a bean's roots

materials.item: a whole plant of a bean-family crop with roots, such as groundnut, pea, tur, chana or horse gram, with some soil on the roots
a magnifying glass, a tray and a bowl of water to wash the roots
a clean sharp blade or knife, used only by a grown-up
a white plate and a notebook

activities.safety: A grown-up does the cutting with the blade. Wash hands after handling roots and soil.

schedule.what: Wash the roots. Find the nodules. A grown-up cuts one open. Look inside.

activities.record: Draw the root with the nodules. Count them. Draw one cut nodule and its colour.
activities.context: In this activity, you look at the roots of a bean-family plant and find the lumps where helpful bacteria live and fix nitrogen.

setup.art: A groundnut plant with the roots shaken and gently rinsed in a bowl of water.
setup.caption: 1. Gently wash the soil off the roots of a bean-family plant.

setup.art: A root laid on a white plate with several small round lumps circled in pencil, and a magnifying glass above.
setup.caption: 2. Find the round lumps on the roots. These are nodules.

setup.art: A grown-up cutting one nodule in half with a blade to show a pink centre.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up cuts one open. Look at the colour inside.

flow.do: Show the plant and ask your child what lives on the roots. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write the answer.
flow.say: Some plants have helpers on their roots. What might you see? What do you think the helpers do?
flow.kid: Look at the roots. What might live there? Guess.
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. You can get a whole groundnut plant from a market in the groundnut season, or from a field. Moong or chana plants grown in garden soil for five weeks can show small nodules. Potting mix from a bag often has no bacteria, and so no nodules. This is the activity most likely to fail at home, so check a market or a farmer's field for a pulled-up plant. If you find no nodules, look at the pictures and say honestly what you did not see. Two to four children can share one plant and one magnifier, and take turns to count.
flow.context: This is the first step of Find the Pink Factories. You guess before you look.

flow.do: Wash the roots gently in a bowl of water. Look for round lumps along the roots. Count them. Do not pull them off.
flow.say: Look closely at the roots. Do you see small round lumps? Count them. Don't pull them off, as they are part of the root.
flow.kid: Wash the roots. Look for round lumps. Count them.

ask.q: What do you think the lumps are? Are they part of the plant?
good: They are lumps made by the plant.
They are houses for bacteria.
They are swellings.

flow.parent: Nodules are firm, round lumps stuck to the root. They are not the same as the long, thin hairs or the root's own swellings. Old, dead nodules look grey or green inside.
flow.context: In this step, you wash the roots and find the nodules.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts one nodule in half. Look at the colour inside. Pink or red means the nodule is working. Draw it.
flow.say: A grown-up cuts one lump in half. What colour is the inside? A pink inside means the bacteria are fixing nitrogen.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts a nodule. What colour is the inside?

ask.q: The plant gives sugar to the bacteria. What does the plant get back?
good: Nitrogen that the plant can use.
Food for making leaves and seeds.
A kind of fertiliser.

check.q: Why does a farmer grow dal after rice in the same field?
options: The dal plants and their root bacteria put nitrogen back into the soil
The dal plants make the soil harder
The dal plants use up all the minerals
The dal plants keep birds away
check.why: Rice takes nitrogen out of the soil. A legume with root nodules fixes nitrogen from the air and leaves some behind for the next crop.

flow.parent: A pink or red centre shows the nodule is active. A white or green centre shows it is old or not working. A cut nodule can look dry within minutes. If you have no blade, a grown-up can squash one nodule between two clean fingernails and look for a pink smear. Keep the plate in good light.
flow.context: In this step, a grown-up cuts a nodule and you look inside.

activities.title: Plant Check-up Walk: read the leaves and feel the soil

materials.item: a notebook, a pencil and a clipboard or a book to write on
a magnifying glass
a plant clue chart, drawn by your child from the clues in the Plant Doctor game

schedule.what: Visit five plants at home, in the balcony or on the street. Note the leaves, the soil and the light. Make a guess for each.

activities.record: A table with five plants: where the plant grows, which leaves look unusual, soil wet or dry by the finger test, light, and your best guess.
activities.context: In this activity, you go on a walk to check five real plants like a plant doctor. You read the clues and say what each plant needs.

setup.art: A child with a notebook looking closely at a yellow-leafed plant in a pot on a balcony.
setup.caption: 1. Choose a plant. Look at the leaves, old and new.

setup.art: A child pressing a finger two knuckles deep into the soil of a pot, with a notebook table.
setup.caption: 2. Do the finger test on the soil. Is it wet or dry?

setup.art: A completed table of five plants with a guess for each, and a clue chart beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Write your best guess for each plant.

flow.do: Draw a table with five rows. Write the columns: plant, leaves, soil, light, my guess. Explain the finger test.
flow.say: We will check five plants like a plant doctor. For each one, look at the leaves, feel the soil and think about the light.
flow.kid: Draw a table. Look at five plants. Do the finger test on each soil.
flow.parent: Play Plant Doctor first, or copy a few clues from its tokens. Two to four children can each take different plants, and then compare guesses. Only touch plants that belong to you or that you have permission to touch. For the finger test, push a clean finger two knuckles deep into the soil, away from the stem. Wash hands afterwards.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Plant Check-up Walk. You set up your table.

flow.do: Visit each plant in turn. Check the old and new leaves. Do the finger test. Note the light. Write a guess for each.
flow.say: Look at the old leaves and the new leaves. Are any pale or spotted? Is the soil wet or dry two knuckles deep? Is the light bright or dim?
flow.kid: Look at the old and new leaves. Test the soil. Write a guess.

ask.q: Which plant looks healthiest? What clues tell you?
good: Dark green leaves and firm stems.
New leaves are growing.
The soil is damp but not soaked.

flow.parent: Most plants you meet will be fine. Do not worry if you find no problem. Healthy plants are a useful result too. If a plant has yellow leaves, check for wet soil, a blocked hole and sun before you guess a mineral shortage.

check.q: You find a plant with yellow leaves and soaked soil that smells sour. What should you check first?
options: Whether the pot drains, and whether the roots are drowning
Whether to water the plant more
Whether to move the plant into the dark
check.why: Soaked, sour soil points to roots without air. More fertiliser or water would make things worse. Fix the drainage first.

flow.context: In this step, you visit the plants and record what you see.

flow.do: Share your guesses with a family member. Which plant had the clearest clues? Which was hardest to guess?
flow.say: Tell me about your plants. Which clue was the clearest? Which plant was hardest to guess? What more would you need to know?
flow.kid: Tell someone about your plants. Which was hardest to guess?
flow.think: A plant doctor never knows for sure from one look. What else could you check to be more certain?
flow.context: In this step, you share your guesses and think about what else you would check.

activities.title: Liebig's Bottle: the shortest plank sets the level

materials.item: a clean 1-litre plastic bottle, with the top third cut off by a grown-up
scissors, a marker and some tape
a jug of water, a small cup to pour with, a tray or a basin, and waterproof clear tape (packing tape works better than masking tape)
paper labels and a ruler

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the bottle with scissors, and smooths the cut edges so they are not sharp.

schedule.what: Make five notches in the rim of a bottle at different heights. Pour water to find the limit. Tape over the lowest notch and pour again.

activities.record: Draw the bottle with its five notches labelled with minerals. Mark where the water level stopped each time. Count how many cups of water the bottle held each time.
activities.context: In this activity, you build a bottle model of the idea that the shortest supply sets how well a plant can grow.

setup.art: A plastic bottle with the top cut off and five notches cut into its rim, each at a different depth, labelled N, P, K, Ca and Fe.
setup.caption: 1. Cut five notches in the rim at different depths. Label them N, P, K, Ca and Fe.

setup.art: A jug pouring water into the bottle, with water spilling out of the lowest notch, N, onto a tray.
setup.caption: 2. Pour water in. It spills out of the lowest notch.

setup.art: A strip of tape mending the lowest notch, and the water rising until it reaches the next lowest notch.
setup.caption: 3. Tape over the lowest notch. The water rises to the next lowest one.

flow.do: Show the bottle and ask your child to guess where the water will spill. Write the guess.
flow.say: Each notch is a mineral. The water is how well the plant can grow. When we fill the bottle, where will the water spill? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: The water level stands for how well the plant grows. Where will the water spill? Why?

ask.q: If you pour more water in, will the water level go higher than the lowest notch?
good: No, it will spill out of the lowest one.
Yes, if I pour fast.
It stays at the lowest notch.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Make the notches at five clearly different heights, 1 to 2 centimetres apart, on the rim of the cut bottle. Label the notches N, P, K, Ca and Fe. Dry the outside before taping. With one child, the child pours and the parent counts. With two to four children, one pours, one tapes, one counts cups and one records. Or each child makes a bottle with different notch heights and predicts where the water will spill.
flow.context: This is the first step of Liebig's Bottle. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Pour water slowly into the bottle until it spills. Mark the level and count the cups that went in. Tape over the lowest notch. Pour again. Mark the new level and count the cups again.
flow.say: Pour until the water spills. Tape over the lowest notch. Pour again. What happens to the level? Does the next lowest notch decide?
flow.kid: Pour until it spills. Tape the lowest notch. Pour again.

ask.q: What does the lowest notch stand for? What happens when you tape it?
good: It stands for the shortest supply of a mineral.
The level rises to the next one.
The next shortest supply is now the limit.

check.q: A plant has plenty of phosphorus and potassium but very little nitrogen. In the bottle model, what happens when you add more phosphorus?
options: Nothing, because nitrogen is still the lowest notch
The plant grows twice as fast
The water level rises to the top
check.why: The level stays at the lowest notch. Adding more of a mineral that is already plentiful does not help until the shortest one is supplied.

flow.context: In this step, you pour water and find the limit, then tape over the lowest notch.

flow.do: Think about a real plant. Which mineral could be the lowest notch? How would you find out? Write one idea.
flow.say: If this were a real plant, how would a farmer find the lowest notch? What would she test?
flow.kid: How could a farmer find the lowest notch? Write one idea.
flow.think: In a bottle, you can see the lowest notch. A farmer cannot see it in the soil. How could she find it?
flow.context: In this step, you link the model to a real farmer's problem.

activities.title: Air Pipes in a Lotus Stem: how roots in mud get air

materials.item: a piece of lotus stem or lotus root (kamal kakdi) about 10 centimetres long, between two joints, from a market, washed, plus a clean drinking straw and a little atta dough
a bowl of water
a clean sharp knife, used only by a grown-up
a magnifying glass and a notebook

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the stem with the knife. Never put a raw lotus stem in your mouth, because raw water plants can carry germs and parasites. Wash hands afterwards. Blow through a clean drinking straw, not the stem.

schedule.what: A grown-up cuts a slice of lotus stem. Look at the holes. Blow through a long piece in a bowl of water and watch the bubbles.

activities.record: Draw the cut end of the stem and count the holes. Draw the bubbles in the water.
activities.context: In this activity, you look at a lotus stem and find the air channels that carry air down to the roots in the mud.

setup.art: A grown-up slicing a lotus stem and a slice laid flat on a plate with a ring of holes showing.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts a thin slice of lotus stem. Count the holes.

setup.art: A child holding a piece of lotus stem with a straw pushed into one end, sealed with dough, and the other end in a bowl of water.
setup.caption: 2. Seal a straw into one end with dough. Put the other end in water. Blow gently through the straw.

setup.art: Silver bubbles streaming out of the water end of the stem into the bowl.
setup.caption: 3. Watch for bubbles in the water. The air has travelled along the pipes.

flow.do: Show the lotus stem and ask what the holes might be for. Write the guess.
flow.say: A lotus grows with their roots in mud, where there is almost no air. How might the roots get air? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A lotus has roots in mud. How do the roots get air? Guess.
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. If you cannot find lotus stem, look at pictures. A slice of a banana stem, or the leaf stalk of a taro, shows big air spaces too.
flow.context: This is the first step of Air Pipes in a Lotus Stem. You guess before you look.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts a slice. Count the holes. Then the grown-up cuts a fresh piece 10 centimetres long from between two joints, so that both ends are newly cut. Seal a straw into one end with a ball of atta dough. Put the other end into the water and blow gently through the straw.
flow.say: Count the holes in the slice. Now seal the straw into one end and put the other end into the water. Blow gently into the straw. What happens?
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the stem. Count the holes. Blow through the straw into the stem in water.

ask.q: What are the holes for? What happens when you blow?
good: They carry air.
Bubbles come out the other end.
The air goes down to the roots.

check.q: Why do plants that grow in mud, such as lotus and rice, have air channels?
options: To carry oxygen from the leaves down to roots in mud that has none
To make the stems lighter for floating
To store water for dry days
To make the stem easier to eat
check.why: Mud has very little oxygen, but roots still need it. The air channels carry oxygen from the leaves above the water down to the roots.

flow.parent: Cut pieces fresh, because the cut ends dry out. Blow gently. Air passes along a segment but joints often block it, so use one piece between two joints. If no bubbles appear, try another piece, or cut off a little more at the end. A taro (arbi) leaf stalk also works. With one child, the parent cuts and seals, and the child blows. Two to four children take turns, each with their own clean straw.
flow.context: In this step, you look at the holes and blow through the stem.

flow.do: Draw what you saw. Talk about how a pot plant, a rice plant and a lotus get air to their roots.
flow.say: How does a pot plant get air to their roots? How does a rice plant? Are the ways the same?
flow.kid: Draw what you saw. How do roots in mud get air?
flow.think: A mangrove tree grows in salty mud, and sends up pencil-like roots into the air. What might those roots be for?
flow.context: In this step, you draw what you saw and compare different ways plants get air to their roots.

projects.title: From Peels to Plant Food: a compost bottle

materials.item: a clear 2-litre plastic bottle, with the top third cut off and 10 small air holes poked in the sides and bottom by a grown-up
dry leaves or torn newspaper, a few handfuls
vegetable and fruit peels from the kitchen, chopped small. Do not use cooked food, meat, fish, dairy or oily scraps
a handful of garden soil, a spoon of old compost if you have it, and a wooden stick
a spray bottle or cup of water, a tray to catch drips, a piece of cloth and a rubber band
a notebook, a ruler and a marker

projects.safety: A grown-up cuts the bottle and makes the holes. Wash hands after touching compost. Do not put your nose close to the heap. Sniff gently from a distance. Keep the bottle away from food and from small children who might put the compost in their mouths. Anyone with asthma or a mould allergy should not handle the compost, and a grown-up should wear a mask when stirring it if the heap looks mouldy.

schedule.what: Build the compost bottle in layers. Mark the starting height. Cover the top with cloth.
Stir with a stick. Check that it feels like a wrung-out sponge. Write what you see and smell.
Stir. Measure the height. Add water or dry leaves if needed.
Stir. Measure the height. Draw the colours.
Look, smell and measure. Compare with day 1. Write what the decomposers did.

projects.record: A table with the date, the height of the heap, the smell, the colour and anything alive you see. Draw the bottle on days 1, 21 and 35.
projects.context: In this project, you turn kitchen peels and dry leaves into compost in a bottle over five weeks. You watch decomposers turn waste into plant food.

setup.art: A bottle with its top cut off and air holes poked in, standing on a tray.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts a bottle and pokes air holes. Stand it on a tray.

setup.art: Layers in the bottle: dry leaves at the bottom, kitchen peels, a handful of soil, and a spritz of water.
setup.caption: 2. Fill in layers: dry leaves, peels, soil. Spray with water.

setup.art: The bottle covered with a cloth tied with a rubber band, a stick used to stir, and a marker line showing the starting level.
setup.caption: 3. Mark the level. Cover with cloth. Stir every few days.

flow.do: Show the peels, the leaves and the bottle. Ask for a guess and a reason about what will happen over five weeks. Write it down.
flow.say: We will fill a bottle with peels and leaves and leave it for five weeks. What do you think will happen? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: We will leave peels and leaves in a bottle for five weeks. What will happen? Why?

ask.q: Who do you think will do the work in the bottle?
good: Tiny living things like bacteria and fungi.
Worms.
Nobody. It will just dry out.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. To compare, two to four children can each build a bottle with one change (no dry leaves, large pieces of peel, or no soil starter) and compare after five weeks. One child alone can build two bottles. Any guess with a reason is a good start. The bacteria and fungi are already on the peels and leaves.
flow.context: This is the first step of the compost bottle project. You guess before you build.

flow.do: A grown-up cuts the bottle and pokes holes. Layer a handful of dry leaves, a handful of chopped peels, and a handful of soil. Repeat. Spray with water until damp.
flow.say: Build it in layers: dry leaves, then peels, then soil. Then do the three layers again. Spray with water until it feels like a wrung-out sponge.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts the bottle. Add layers of leaves, peels and soil. Spray with water.
flow.parent: Cut the peels small, which helps them rot faster. Mix about two parts dry leaves to one part peels. The heap should be damp but not dripping. If it is too wet, it will smell sour, because the gaps fill with water and run out of air. Add dry leaves, and stir.

check.q: Why do we poke air holes in the bottle and stir the heap?
options: The decomposers need oxygen to work and rot the waste
The holes are for the water to evaporate
The stick makes the peels colourful
The air keeps the bottle cool
check.why: Most decomposers use oxygen to break the peels down. Without air, the heap goes sour and slimy. Holes and stirring let the air in.

flow.context: In this step, you build the compost bottle in layers.

flow.do: Cover the top with cloth. Mark the starting height of the heap on the bottle. Put the bottle on a tray in a warm, shady place.
flow.say: Cover the top with a cloth. Mark the height of the heap. Put it somewhere warm and shady. We will look again in three days.
flow.kid: Cover the top. Mark the height. Put it in a warm, shady place.
flow.context: In this step, you cover the bottle and mark its starting height.

flow.do: On the checking days, stir the heap, measure the height and write down the smell and colour. On day 35, compare with day 1.
flow.say: Stir the heap. Measure the height. How does it smell? What colour is it? Has it shrunk? Who did that?
flow.kid: Stir the heap. Measure it. Smell it gently. Write what you find.

ask.q: The heap has shrunk and turned dark. Where did the material go?
good: Some became carbon dioxide and water that went into the air.
The decomposers ate it and breathed it out.
Some turned into dark compost.

flow.parent: In warm weather, the heap usually shrinks, turns dark and smells earthy within 4 to 8 weeks, and the peels are mostly gone. A small bottle may need 2 to 3 months to finish. It may be slower in cool weather. If small flies appear, cover the bottle with cloth and add dry leaves. If the heap smells like rotten eggs, it is too wet and short of air. Stir it and add dry leaves. The compost is ready when you cannot see the peels any more.
flow.think: The heap got smaller. The matter was not destroyed. Where did the carbon in the peels go?
flow.context: In this step, you check the compost bottle through the weeks and say what the decomposers did.

challenges.title: The Pot That Never Drowns: design a pot that drains well and still holds water
challenges.problem: Design a pot from recycled things that lets extra water out in a heavy monsoon shower, so the roots never drown, but that still keeps some water for a hot summer day. Test it with 300 millilitres of water poured in over 10 seconds.
constraints: Use only recycled things, such as plastic bottles, tins, cups, stones, sand and coconut husk.
Do not use electricity or any pump.
Fill your pot to the same level with the same soil for every test.
After the test, at least 100 millilitres of the water must stay in the soil, and at least 100 millilitres must drain out within 2 minutes.
materials: a plastic bottle or tin, with the sides and holes cut or poked by a grown-up
garden soil, sand, small stones and coconut husk or dry leaves
a measuring jug, a tray and a clock
a saucer or a second tray to catch the water
bricks or blocks to lift the pot off the saucer
general: A pot with several holes in the bottom and a layer of small stones at the bottom.
A pot raised on two bricks, so that the water drains into the saucer and never touches the pot.
Soil mixed with sand and coconut husk to open up more gaps.
creative: A two-part pot, with the soil in an upper bottle and a water store in a lower bottle, joined by a strip of cloth that pulls up water as the soil dries.
Side holes a little above the bottom, so a small pool of water stays low for dry days.
A bed of coconut husk in a ring around the roots, which holds water like a sponge and still lets air in.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your design. Build it and test it with 300 millilitres. Measure the water that drains out and the water that stays. Change one thing and test again. Which design worked best? Why do you think so?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about roots, air and water. You build a pot that stops roots drowning and still holds enough water.

setup.art: A child sketching three pot designs: a bottle with holes, a pot on bricks and a two-part self-watering pot.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch some pot designs on paper.

setup.art: A bottle pot filled with soil and placed over a tray, with a jug pouring 300 millilitres onto the soil.
setup.caption: 2. Build your pot. Pour in 300 millilitres of water over 10 seconds.

setup.art: A measuring jug showing the water that drained into the tray after two minutes, and a hand pressing the soil to feel how damp it is.
setup.caption: 3. Measure what drained out. Feel how damp the soil is.

flow.do: Read the problem and the rules together. Ask your child to sketch two or three pot designs. Write down a guess of how much water will drain out.
flow.say: Your pot must let extra water out, but keep some for a dry day. How could you do both? Draw some ideas first.
flow.kid: Your pot must drain but still hold some water. Draw some ideas first.

ask.q: What makes water drain out of a pot? What makes it stay in?
good: Holes at the bottom let water out.
Sand and stones let water run through.
Fine soil and husk hold water like a sponge.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Pot That Never Drowns challenge. You plan your pot.

flow.do: Build your first pot. Fill it with soil to a marked level. Pour 300 millilitres of water over 10 seconds. Measure what drains out after 2 minutes.
flow.say: Build your pot. Pour in 300 millilitres. Wait two minutes. How much drained out? How much stayed?
flow.kid: Build your pot. Pour in 300 millilitres. Measure what drains out.

ask.q: How much drained out? How much stayed in the soil?
good: More than half drained.
Less than 100 millilitres stayed.
Hardly anything drained.

flow.parent: The water that stays is 300 minus what drained out, though a little will cling to the cup and the tray. A grown-up cuts the pot and pokes the holes, and smooths any sharp edges. Pour slowly onto the middle of the soil, because water that runs over the rim counts as drained. A plain bottle with a few holes usually drains about 50 to 150 millilitres. More holes or sand drain more. Coconut husk or cocopeat holds more. Let the soil start dry each time, or note if it started damp. Two to four children can each build a pot, and then compare. One child can build a second pot after the first.

check.q: In a pot, 300 millilitres of water were poured in, and 220 millilitres drained out. About how much water stayed in the soil?
check.why: 300 minus 220 is 80. The soil kept about 80 millilitres, which fills some of the gaps and leaves the others full of air.

flow.context: In this step, you build your first pot and test it.

flow.do: Change one thing about your pot and test it again. Compare the two tests. Write which design is better and why.
flow.say: Change just one thing, such as the number of holes or the soil mix. Test again. Which design worked better? Why?
flow.kid: Change one thing. Test again. Which design is better?
flow.think: A pot for a cactus and a pot for a rice plant need very different drainage. How would you change your design for each?
flow.context: In this step, you improve your pot and compare the two tests.

challenges.title: Rotation Plan: feed the soil for six seasons
challenges.problem: A farmer has one field with 5 points of nitrogen in the soil. Each season, she grows one crop. Plan six seasons to get the most harvest points, without the nitrogen in the field ever falling below zero.
constraints: A crop can be grown only if the field has at least as many nitrogen points as the crop uses.
Rice uses 2 nitrogen points and gives 4 harvest points. Wheat uses 2 and gives 4. Maize uses 3 and gives 5.
Black gram, a dal, adds 2 nitrogen points and gives 2 harvest points. Groundnut adds 1 nitrogen point and gives 3 harvest points.
A bag of fertiliser adds 3 nitrogen points but costs 3 harvest points. You may use it once in a season, before you grow the crop.
materials: 6 small squares of paper for the seasons
dried beans or buttons for the nitrogen points
a copy of the crop rules
general: Grow rice, then black gram, then rice, then black gram, and so on. The dal puts back what the rice takes.
Grow the high-value crops first and use fertiliser when the nitrogen runs low.
creative: Mix the crops in a smart order: rice, then black gram, then maize, then groundnut, then rice, then black gram.
Plan around a neighbour: share the fertiliser bag between two fields.
Add a fallow season, in which the field is left to rest and nothing is grown.
challenges.your_turn: Plan your six seasons. Keep a running total for the nitrogen and the harvest points. Then try to beat your score. Explain why alternating crops keeps the soil rich.
challenges.context: This is a paper design challenge about crop rotation. You use nitrogen points to plan six seasons and find a plan that keeps the soil rich.

setup.art: A row of six squares for six seasons, each with a crop picture, and a column of beans standing for nitrogen points.
setup.caption: 1. Draw six seasons. Put 5 beans for the nitrogen at the start.

setup.art: A hand moving beans away for a rice crop and adding beans for a black gram crop.
setup.caption: 2. Each season, take beans away for cereals. Add beans for dal.

setup.art: A score sheet with the crops in order, the beans left each season and the harvest total.
setup.caption: 3. Write the crop, the nitrogen left and the harvest points for each season.

flow.do: Read the rules. Ask your child why a farmer might grow dal after rice. Write the answer.
flow.say: Rice takes nitrogen from the soil. Black gram puts it back. What plan do you think will give the most food over six seasons? Why?
flow.kid: Rice takes nitrogen. Dal puts it back. What plan gives the most food?

ask.q: What happens if the farmer grows only rice for six seasons?
good: The nitrogen runs out after two seasons.
The rice stops growing well.
She has to buy fertiliser.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Rotation Plan challenge. You think about nitrogen.

flow.do: Try a plan. Write each season's crop, the nitrogen left and the harvest points. Add up the harvest. Then try a second plan.
flow.say: Use the dried beans or buttons as nitrogen points. Go season by season. Take beans away for a cereal and add beans for a dal. Never let the beans fall below zero. Add up the harvest points.
flow.kid: Plan six seasons. Count the nitrogen points with your beans. Add up the harvest points.

ask.q: What was your total? Could you beat it?
good: Twenty or more.
I used the fertiliser once.
I mixed in groundnut.
