quiz.p: About what share of a good, loose soil is gaps that hold air and water?
opts: Between a third and a half
Almost none
All of it
One in every hundred parts
quiz.why: Soil is grains with gaps between them. In loose garden soil, the gaps can be nearly half of the volume. Packed soil has less.

quiz.p: A plant in a pot droops. The soil is soaked and smells sour. What is the most likely problem?
opts: The roots are drowning for lack of air
The plant needs more water
The plant needs more fertiliser
The plant needs less light
quiz.why: Soaked soil has no air in its gaps. Roots without oxygen cannot work, and begin to rot, which gives the sour smell. More water or fertiliser would make this worse.

quiz.p: Which three minerals do plants need in the largest amounts?
opts: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium
Iron, zinc and copper
Sodium, chlorine and calcium
Carbon, oxygen and hydrogen
quiz.why: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium are the three numbers on a bag of fertiliser. Iron, zinc and copper are needed in tiny amounts. Carbon, oxygen and hydrogen come from air and water.

quiz.p: A soil has plenty of phosphorus and potassium but very little nitrogen. What limits the crop?
opts: Nitrogen, the shortest supply
Phosphorus, the most plentiful
Potassium, the most plentiful
Nothing limits it
quiz.why: Growth is held back by the shortest supply. The plentiful minerals do not help until the shortest one is added.

quiz.p: Plants grown with their roots in water that holds a few mineral salts, and no soil, grew well and made seeds. What did this show?
opts: Soil gives minerals, water and support, but the plant makes their own food
Plants eat soil
Plants do not need minerals
Plants need humus
quiz.why: The plants had no soil and no humus, and still grew. So the plant's food is made in the leaves. The soil supplies minerals, water and a place to hold on.

quiz.p: What do bacteria in a bean's root nodules give the plant, and what do they get from the plant?
opts: They give nitrogen and get sugar
They give sugar and get nitrogen
They give water and get light
They give nothing and get a home
quiz.why: The bacteria fix nitrogen from the air into a form the plant can use. The plant gives them sugar from photosynthesis. Both sides gain.

quiz.p: Why can a plant not use the nitrogen gas that makes up most of the air?
opts: Its atoms are locked together tightly, and it must be fixed first
It is too heavy
It is poisonous
It is the wrong colour
quiz.why: The two atoms in a nitrogen molecule are joined by a very strong bond. Only bacteria, lightning and factories can break it and join the nitrogen to other atoms.

quiz.p: What does a fungus on a tree's roots mainly bring to the tree?
opts: Water and minerals such as phosphorus, in return for sugar
Light
Carbon dioxide
Sugar, in return for water
quiz.why: Fungus threads reach farther into the soil than roots, and gather minerals and water. The tree pays with sugar from photosynthesis.

quiz.p: Scientists all agree that trees use fungus networks to care for their young on purpose.
quiz.why: False. Carbon does move between trees linked by fungi, but scientists disagree about how much, and whether the trees do it on purpose. This is still being tested.

quiz.p: A day after a big dose of fertiliser, the leaf edges of a pot plant turn brown and crispy. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Fertiliser salts have burned the roots and leaf edges
The plant needs more fertiliser
The plant has too little water in the saucer
The plant needs less air
quiz.why: Strong fertiliser salts draw water out of roots and scorch the leaf edges. The fix is to flush the pot with plenty of water and use a smaller dose next time.

quiz.p: Which statement about a plant's needs in the soil is correct?
opts: Roots need air as well as water
Roots need only water
Roots need only minerals
Roots need no air because they are underground
quiz.why: Roots are alive and respire, so they need oxygen. The gaps in soil hold the air they breathe. Waterlogged soil has no air.

quiz.p: In 1828, Carl Sprengel described the shortest plank idea, but it became known as Liebig's law. What does this show about science?
opts: Credit does not always go to the first person who found something
The first person always gets the credit
Only famous people can make discoveries
Ideas cannot be named after anyone
quiz.why: Liebig was famous and wrote a best-selling book, so his name stuck. Sprengel had the idea first. Looking back at who found what helps give credit where it is due.

open_questions.q: How much food and water do trees really share through fungus networks?
open_questions.why_open: Some studies find carbon moving between trees. Others say the amounts are too small to matter. More careful tests in real forests are needed.

open_questions.q: Could wheat, rice and maize be given nodules that fix their own nitrogen?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists are working on it, but a nodule needs many genes working together in the right order. Nobody has made it work in a cereal crop.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of tiny living things live in a teaspoon of soil?
open_questions.why_open: Most soil microbes have never been grown in a dish or given a name. New methods read their genes directly, and keep finding kinds that nobody knew.

open_questions.q: How does a root tip combine so many signals, such as water, minerals, touch and gravity, into one decision?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know many of the signals and the chemicals involved. How the root tip puts them all together is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: Did the first plants on land need fungi to survive?
open_questions.why_open: Fossils about 400 million years old show fungi inside early plant roots. Whether the first land plants could have lived without them is not known.

open_questions.q: How can farms keep high harvests while rebuilding soil and saving groundwater?
open_questions.why_open: Many ideas exist, such as crop rotation, compost and less ploughing. Which mix works best in each place is still being tested.

maths.problem: A big pot holds 2,000 millilitres of loose garden soil. In the Soil Breath test, about 45 out of every 100 millilitres of that soil were gaps. About how many millilitres of the pot are gaps?
maths.explain: 2,000 millilitres is 20 lots of 100 millilitres. 20 times 45 is 900. So about 900 millilitres of the pot are gaps, and 1,100 millilitres are grains. When the pot is waterlogged, those 900 millilitres are full of water instead of air.
maths.context: In the Soil Breath test, you find how many millilitres of every 100 millilitres of soil are gaps.
maths.why_maths: Scaling a result from a small cup to a whole pot shows how much air a real plant's roots have to breathe.

maths.problem: Loose soil took in 46 millilitres of water for every 100 millilitres of soil. Packed soil took in 34 millilitres. How many millilitres fewer was that? About what fraction of the loose soil's gaps was lost by packing?
maths.answer: 12 millilitres fewer, about a quarter of the gaps.
maths.explain: 46 take away 34 is 12. 12 out of 46 is a bit more than 12 out of 48, and 12 out of 48 is one quarter. So packing squeezed out about a quarter of the gaps.
maths.context: In the Soil Breath test, you compare loose soil with soil packed down hard.
maths.why_maths: Turning a difference into a fraction shows how large the change is compared with where you started.

maths.problem: In the Pot That Never Drowns challenge, 300 millilitres of water were poured in and 190 millilitres drained into the tray. How many millilitres stayed in the soil? Is that more or less than a half of the water poured in?
maths.answer: 110 millilitres stayed. That is less than half.
maths.explain: 300 take away 190 is 110. Half of 300 is 150. 110 is less than 150, so less than half of the water stayed. The rest drained out, and left room for air.
maths.context: In the Pot That Never Drowns challenge, you pour 300 millilitres of water into a pot and measure what drains out.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting the drained water from the water poured in tells you how much the soil kept, so you can judge the design.

maths.problem: A 50-kilogram bag of fertiliser is labelled 20-10-10. The numbers are percentages of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium. How many kilograms of each are in the bag?
maths.answer: 10 kilograms of nitrogen, 5 kilograms of phosphorus and 5 kilograms of potassium.
maths.explain: 20 percent of 50 is 10, because 50 divided by 5 is 10. 10 percent of 50 is 5, because 50 divided by 10 is 5. So the bag has 10, 5 and 5 kilograms.
maths.why_maths: Percentages on a label tell a farmer how much of each mineral she is really buying.

maths.problem: A made-up price: Bag A is 50 kilograms of 20-10-10 fertiliser and costs 1,000 rupees. Bag B is 50 kilograms of 10-10-10 and costs 700 rupees. Which bag costs less for each kilogram of nitrogen?
maths.answer: Bag A. It costs 100 rupees for each kilogram of nitrogen, and bag B costs 140 rupees.
maths.explain: Bag A holds 10 kilograms of nitrogen. 1,000 divided by 10 is 100 rupees for each kilogram. Bag B holds 5 kilograms of nitrogen. 700 divided by 5 is 140 rupees for each kilogram. A is cheaper for nitrogen, even though the whole bag costs more.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the price by the nitrogen in the bag compares bags fairly, when the shortest mineral is nitrogen.

maths.problem: In the Seedlings Without Soil test, the tallest shoot in jar B was 3 centimetres on day 4, 8 centimetres on day 8, 14 centimetres on day 12 and 22 centimetres on day 18. How much did the shoot grow between each check? Between which two checks did the shoot grow the most per day?
maths.answer: The shoot grew 5, 6 and 8 centimetres. The shoot grew the most per day between day 8 and day 12.
maths.explain: 8 take away 3 is 5. 14 take away 8 is 6. 22 take away 14 is 8. The checks are 4 days, 4 days and 6 days apart. 5 over 4 days is 1.25 centimetres a day. 6 over 4 days is 1.5. 8 over 6 days is about 1.3. So the fastest was between day 8 and day 12.
maths.context: In the Seedlings Without Soil test, you measure the tallest shoot in each jar on several days.
maths.why_maths: Comparing growth per day, not just growth between checks, is fair when the checks are different lengths of time apart.

maths.problem: In the Rotation Plan challenge, a field starts with 5 nitrogen points. The farmer grows rice, which uses 2, then black gram, which adds 2, then maize, which uses 3. How many nitrogen points are left? Could she grow maize again straight away?
maths.answer: 2 nitrogen points are left. She could not grow maize again, because it needs 3.
maths.explain: 5 take away 2 is 3. 3 add 2 is 5. 5 take away 3 is 2. Maize uses 3, and there are only 2 left, so she needs a dal or fertiliser first.
maths.context: In the Rotation Plan challenge, you plan six seasons of crops and keep track of the nitrogen points in the field.
maths.why_maths: Keeping a running total shows when a plan will run out of nitrogen before it happens.

maths.problem: A fertiliser label says to use 5 millilitres for every litre of water. How many millilitres should go into a 300 millilitre jar for the full dose? What about for half of the dose, and for double the dose?
maths.answer: 1.5 millilitres for the full dose, 0.75 for half and 3 for double.
maths.explain: 300 millilitres is 0.3 of a litre. 5 times 0.3 is 1.5. Half of 1.5 is 0.75, and double 1.5 is 3. So with this label, the three jars in the test get 0, 0.75 and 3 millilitres.
maths.context: In the Seedlings Without Soil test, you give one jar a small dose and one a big dose of fertiliser.
maths.why_maths: Scaling a dose to a smaller jar keeps the strength the same, so the test is fair.

maths.problem: In the Soil in a Jar activity, the layers were sand 3 centimetres, silt 2 centimetres and clay 1 centimetre. What fraction of the mineral layers is sand? Which layer is the thinnest, and what could that mean?
maths.answer: Half of the mineral layers are sand. Clay is the thinnest.
maths.explain: The layers add up to 3 plus 2 plus 1, which is 6 centimetres. 3 out of 6 is one half. Clay is only 1 out of 6, so this soil has little clay. A soil with a lot of clay would hold water tightly and have smaller gaps.
maths.context: In the Soil in a Jar activity, you shake soil in water and measure the layers that settle.
maths.why_maths: Writing a layer as a fraction of the whole tells you what the soil is mostly made of, and how it will behave.

roots.context: We have found that half of soil is air, that roots breathe, and that plants trade with bacteria and fungi. Now we ask what this says about empty space and about who we depend on.

deep_truth.truth: In the Soil Breath test, water poured on dry soil pushed out bubbles of air. Between a third and a half of each soil was gaps. Roots grow into these gaps and breathe there. So the gaps in soil are as much the plant's home as the grains.
deep_truth.habit: We think of soil as the solid stuff, and of the space between the grains as nothing. For a root, the gaps are where the air is. So what we call nothing is nearly half of the root's home.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Soil Breath test, 100 millilitres of dry soil took in about 35 to 50 millilitres of water before the water reached the top, and bubbles of air rushed out. Packed soil took in less. A pot with all its gaps full of water drowns the roots. If your own numbers differ, write them down as they are and test again.

three.who_am_i: Your lungs also work by having space inside them, full of air. Your body, like soil, is partly solid and partly space, and the breathing happens in the space.
three.what_is_life: No living being works alone. A bean has bacteria in her roots, a tree has fungi, and the soil has millions of tiny helpers. Life is a web of trades.
three.what_is_this_world: The soil under our feet is half empty space, and that space is full of air and life. What looks solid and still is full of room and movement.

roots.thread: Soil looks like one solid thing. Pour water on it and you find that nearly half of it is air. The roots live in the gaps, and the bacteria and fungi do too. The gaps are not wasted space. They are where the work happens. The gaps and the grains are two parts of one working soil, just as a plant's breathing and a plant's body are two parts of one living plant. The plant also depends on partners they cannot see, who live in the same gaps. Take away the gaps, or the partners, and the plant cannot live.

teachings.teaching: A verse calls the Earth a mother. It says, 'The Earth is my mother, and I am her child.'
teachings.link: A plant's body is built from air, water and a pinch of the Earth's minerals. We eat plants, so we, too, are built from the Earth's soil.

teachings.teaching: The Tamil poet Thiruvalluvar wrote that if the farmer ploughs so well that the soil dries down to a quarter of its weight, the crop will grow even without a handful of manure.
teachings.link: Ploughing opens the soil and lets air into the gaps. Thiruvalluvar saw, long before roots were studied, that air in the soil matters.

science.text: Between a third and a half of a good loose soil is gaps, and roots need the oxygen in them.
Fungi on roots bring plants minerals and water, and bacteria in nodules fix nitrogen. Both trade with the plant for sugar.
How much carbon and how many signals move between trees through fungus networks is still argued about.
Whether a cereal crop could be given nodules and fix their own nitrogen is unknown.

other_view.view: The gaps in soil are a physical property called porosity, which can be measured. The gaps are not a home for anything. They are only empty volume between grains. Saying that the empty space is part of the plant's home is a way of speaking, and does not add to the science.

how_we_found_out.story: In the early 1800s, many farm scientists believed in the humus theory: that plants feed on humus, the dark rotting stuff in soil. In 1840, the chemist Justus von Liebig argued that plants take only simple minerals from the soil, and carbon dioxide from the air. A German scientist, Carl Sprengel, had written something similar in 1828, but few listened. Around 1860, two German scientists, Julius Sachs and Wilhelm Knop, tested the idea. They grew plants in glass jars with their roots in water. The water held only a few simple mineral salts, and there was no soil and no humus. The plants grew well, flowered and made seeds. So humus was not the plant's food. The soil gives minerals, water and a place to hold on. The plant makes their own food in their leaves.
how_we_found_out.who: Julius Sachs and Wilhelm Knop, German plant scientists, building on Carl Sprengel and Justus von Liebig
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many farm scientists believed that a plant feeds on humus, the dark rotting matter in soil. Plants grown in water with only mineral salts, and no humus, grew well and made seeds.

Tap water has some minerals. Roots Need to Breathe: the difference may be small. The nodule activity needs a whole legume plant, and may fail. Do not put raw lotus stem in the mouth.
